item.title: Andrews Upsets Graham in South Carolina, Flipping a Crucial Seat
item.description:
Dr. Annie Andrews, a pediatrician and a Democrat, has defeated Senator Darline Graham, the South Carolina Republican appointed to fill her late brother’s seat, according to The Associated Press. The victory, projected earlier by The New York Times, is a stunning upset in a deeply conservative state, improving Democrats’ chances of winning Senate control.

Ms. Graham’s defeat reflected a toxic political environment for the G.O.P. and the limits of President Trump’s appeal, even in a solidly Republican state where he had been popular.

South Carolina had not been expected to be a midterm battleground. The state had not elected a Democrat to the Senate since 1998, and Mr. Trump won it handily in three presidential elections.

But Senator Lindsey Graham’s death in July upended politics in the state, and Ms. Graham’s selection as his replacement created an opening for Democrats. Both parties spent millions of dollars on the race, and with polls showing remarkably close margins, Mr. Trump traveled to the state three times to try to support Ms. Graham’s campaign.

Given the president’s growing national unpopularity, Dr. Andrews, 45, worked to transform Ms. Graham’s close alliance with him into a liability. She attacked Mr. Trump’s policies for causing costs to rise, blamed Republicans for embracing his agenda and argued that Ms. Graham, who relied on the president’s endorsement to win her primary, would be overly beholden to him.

Democrats are likely to have a Senate majority of four or more seats. They won, or are favored to win, virtually every Senate battleground state.

Though Dr. Andrews herself has never won public office, she also argued that Ms. Graham, who had no political experience before being named a senator, was unqualified and had been improperly anointed as Mr. Graham’s successor.

“Nobody in Washington recruited me to run,” Dr. Andrews told hundreds of supporters gathered in Charleston on Tuesday night. “Nobody handed me a seat in the United States Senate. And nobody wrote me a script. I owe no one in Washington anything.”

The crowd partied for hours in excited anticipation of Dr. Andrews’s victory. They greeted her to shouts of “Annie!” when she finally took the stage. “You have shown the nation what is possible,” she said.

When South Carolina’s Republican governor, Henry McMaster, named a grieving Ms. Graham to the Senate seat, many expected her to be a short-term caretaker. Though she had served as the commissioner of a state agency for blind residents, Ms. Graham had little public profile and had never run for office.

But Mr. Trump, who had been close with Mr. Graham, urged his sister to run as his permanent replacement. He endorsed Ms. Graham in a competitive primary election, then put the weight of his political operation behind getting her elected.

Yet the Republican primary provided an early warning sign for Ms. Graham about the limits of Mr. Trump’s clout. Even in the solidly Republican state, Mr. Trump’s endorsement could not spare her from a runoff election. A stumble on national security during a primary debate raised concerns about her qualifications for office.

After sitting on the sidelines of the midterm elections, Mr. Trump took one of his earliest steps back onto the campaign trail with a rally in August in South Carolina to back Ms. Graham in the runoff. But even after she won the primary, Ms. Graham faced skepticism from the conservative wing of the party.

Dr. Andrews tried to court independent voters unsatisfied with the president and Republicans who were dismayed by Ms. Graham’s ascent. She focused on the economy, highlighting health care in particular.

Ms. Graham and Republicans sought to paint Dr. Andrews as too liberal for South Carolina, pointing in particular to her previous backing of an assault weapons ban; her support for restoring Roe v. Wade, which protected abortion rights; and past support for transgender people.

The last issue became a particular focus. As he tried to drum up conservative support for Ms. Graham, Mr. Trump repeatedly used an anti-transgender slur against Dr. Andrews, who was so besieged by attacks on the issue that she released an ad directly responding to them.

item.title: Democrat Flips Republican-Leaning House Seat in Kentucky
item.description:
Zach Dembo, a Democratic former federal prosecutor and Navy veteran, was elected to an open House seat in Central Kentucky’s Sixth District on Tuesday, according to The Associated Press, delivering an upset in a traditionally conservative stronghold as Republicans struggled with President Trump’s waning popularity.

Mr. Dembo’s victory against Dr. Ralph Alvarado, a physician and former state senator who was backed by President Trump, was a signal of Democratic strength in a district that voted heavily for Mr. Trump two years ago.

The seat had been vacated by Representative Andy Barr, a Republican making a Senate bid to replace Senator Mitch McConnell, who is retiring.

Democrats invested heavily in Mr. Dembo’s campaign, which was included in the Democratic House campaign arm’s “Red to Blue” program. The party establishment viewed his background — he is an ex-military serviceman, an alumnus of the Justice Department and a former official in the administration of Gov. Andy Beshear of Kentucky, a popular Democrat — as an asset.

By contrast, Dr. Alvarado was shadowed by his ties to former Gov. Matt Bevin, Mr. Beshear’s predecessor, whose single term was marked by discord and conflict.

Mr. Dembo, a ninth-generation Kentuckian raised in Lexington, traces his family roots to the 1700s, when generations of his ancestors were farmers. A graduate of Stanford University, he joined the Teach for America program after college and spent two years working as an English teacher in the underserved Mississippi Delta.

He later earned his law degree from the University of Michigan and served for more than four years on active duty as an officer in the Judge Advocate General’s Corps of the U.S. Navy. In 2017, he became a federal prosecutor in the Justice Department’s Civil Rights Division. He returned to Kentucky in 2020, when Mr. Beshear appointed him as legislative director.

Mr. Dembo served as an assistant U.S. attorney in Lexington, but resigned in May 2025 over what he said was concern over the politicization of the justice system under the Trump administration.

His House campaign prioritized ending the war in Iran to reduce gas prices, which Dr. Alvarado, in a break with Mr. Trump, also expressed support for later in his campaign. Mr. Dembo criticized Mr. Trump’s signature domestic policy law, which was passed and signed into law in 2025. He specifically denounced the act’s cuts to Medicaid and its tax breaks for the ultrawealthy.

Mr. Dembo called for the restoration of subsidies provided by the Obama-era Affordable Care Act that expired at the end of last year and supported a public option for health insurance. Dr. Alvarado has criticized the Affordable Care Act.

item.title: 5 Things to Know About Democrat Annie Andrews, South Carolina’s Next Senator
item.description:
In a stunning upset in one of the most conservative states in the nation, Dr. Annie Andrews, a Democrat, will defeat Senator Darline Graham, a Republican, to represent South Carolina in the Senate, according to a projection by The New York Times.

Before Tuesday, a Democrat had not come within even nine percentage points of winning a Senate race this century. Dr. Andrews’s victory amounted to a stark rejection of Ms. Graham, who was appointed to the Senate after her brother, Senator Lindsey Graham, died this summer, and was a significant blow to President Trump, who campaigned heavily on Ms. Graham’s behalf.

Here are five things to know about Dr. Andrews.

1. She is a pediatrician.

Dr. Andrews is a pediatrician who made health care the central issue of her campaign. At stops across the state, she slammed Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. for his stance on vaccines and argued that Republican cuts to Medicare and Medicaid spending had blocked critical access to care for South Carolinians.

She is also a mother of three who resides in a suburb of Charleston. She consistently invoked her own children to explain her focus on keeping South Carolina’s children healthy.

2. She faced attacks for her past views on transgender issues.

Ms. Graham’s most consistent attacks against Dr. Andrews involved her past comments in support of transgender people.

Dr. Andrews has supported prescribing puberty blockers and hormone treatment for children, and she previously argued against a bill that barred transgender athletes from girls’ and women’s sports. She softened some of her language during the campaign.

Dr. Andrews also worked extensively with Moms Demand Action, a gun control advocacy group.

3. She was critical of her party.

In an interview earlier this fall, Dr. Andrews declined to name a single Democratic politician whom she wanted to campaign on her behalf. On the trail, she was almost as quick to criticize the Democratic Party as she was the Republican Party.

“By me winning, I don’t consider it a win for Democrats,” she said in an interview with The New York Times in September. “I consider it a win for South Carolina, because this Senate seat belongs to the people of South Carolina.”

4. She had a spending advantage.

Dr. Andrews out-raised and outspent Ms. Graham, who struggled to fund-raise after bruising primary and runoff elections.

Since the summer, Dr. Andrews also held far more events across South Carolina than Ms. Graham, who was largely focused on learning the ropes in Washington.

5. Call it a comeback.

In 2022, Dr. Andrews challenged Representative Nancy Mace, a Republican, for South Carolina’s First District — but lost by 14 points.

When she first entered the Senate race this cycle, the Republican she was running against was Mr. Graham, and few thought she had a chance of winning the seat.

She remained an underdog after Ms. Graham filled the seat and sought re-election, given the conservative makeup of the state. On Tuesday, she pulled off the upset.

item.title: Deb Haaland Is Elected New Mexico’s Governor, a Historic Victory
item.description:
Deb Haaland, the former congresswoman and interior secretary, will be the nation’s first female Native American governor after she cruised to victory in New Mexico on Tuesday night, according to The Associated Press. Ms. Haaland shrugged off a challenge from a Republican who had rejected negative campaigning.

Ms. Haaland’s victory extended Democratic dominance in the state, which has historically swung between parties but has lately pulled left. En route to her historic win, Ms. Haaland pledged to make New Mexico a capital of resistance to President Trump’s administration.

“Donald Trump thinks he knows something about New Mexico,” Ms. Haaland said at a campaign event in Portales, a small city on the state’s far-eastern flank, in September. “We need to make life more affordable for New Mexicans because we have a president in office who has no clue how we live.”

Ms. Haaland, a member of the Laguna Pueblo, is beloved for breaking barriers. She has racked up a series of firsts since the moment she entered politics: the first Native person to chair a major political party in New Mexico, one of the first two Native American women elected to Congress and the first Native American cabinet secretary, a position she took during the Biden administration.

Her campaign drew national support, helping her raise about $20 million during the primary and general elections. That was more than 10 times what her opponent, Gregg Hull, managed.

Mr. Hull, the former mayor of Rio Rancho, a fast-growing suburb of Albuquerque, was hoping to beat the odds and become the first Republican to win a statewide race in a decade. But in the end, his campaign was perhaps most notable for what he refused to do: go low. In today’s era of bitter and personal political attacks, Mr. Hull vowed to be a nice guy.

It was a striking contrast to Ms. Haaland’s Democratic primary opponent, Sam Bregman, the district attorney of New Mexico’s most populous county, who attacked Ms. Haaland relentlessly. But Ms. Haaland drubbed Mr. Bregman by nearly 45 points.

Ms. Haaland, who takes over from Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham, a term-limited Democrat, will have no shortage of pressing and persistent problems to tackle. New Mexico’s education system is among the nation’s worst performing, and its rates of violent crime and drug overdoses are higher than just about anywhere else.

item.title: Acton Wins Governor’s Race in Ohio
item.description:
After a high-spending race that plumbed the depths of political attacks, Dr. Amy Acton, a Democrat who served during the pandemic as Ohio’s chief public health officer, has been elected the state’s next governor, becoming the first woman to win the office, The Associated Press reported on Tuesday.

She defeated Vivek Ramaswamy, a Republican who made a fortune in pharmaceutical start-ups and had President Trump’s endorsement. She is only the second Democrat to win the governor’s office in Ohio in 35 years.

It was a remarkable achievement for Dr. Acton, 60, whose troubled childhood was thrust into the center of the campaign in its final weeks. Her candidacy had initially seemed like a long shot, given Ohio’s longtime Republican leanings and Mr. Ramaswamy’s canyon-deep pockets.

Though her daily briefings early during the Covid pandemic had been well-received, observers of the race wondered if unpleasant memories of that time, and of unpopular government interventions to prevent Covid’s spread, would become liabilities for her campaign.

But as endorsements piled up for Mr. Ramaswamy, Dr. Acton stuck to a message focused on the high cost of living, emphasizing her roots in the tough-luck city of Youngstown in contrast with her opponent’s enormous wealth.

The mood of Ohio voters began to turn as prices stayed stubbornly high and the Ramaswamy campaign released a series of intensely personal attack ads, including one in late October that featured Dr. Acton’s estranged mother, Donna Arthur, calling her a liar.

The ad drew national condemnation and refocused attention on her family’s troubled history. In 1978, a grand jury had indicted Ms. Arthur’s second husband — Dr. Acton’s stepfather — on charges of raping Dr. Acton, who was 12 at the time. He and Ms. Arthur then fled Ohio, and Dr. Acton and her mother have not spoken since.

People across the political spectrum expressed sympathy for Dr. Acton, though Mr. Ramaswamy and Mr. Trump defended the ad.

The ad may have been a final straw for some undecided voters, but Dr. Acton had been leading in many polls before it ran. At a time of economic discontent, she supported putting more restrictions on the building of data centers, proposed new child tax credits and raised the idea of a gas tax holiday, which Mr. Ramaswamy copied and pushed Republican state lawmakers to approve.

Dr. Acton’s platform did not have the kind of dramatically ambitious ideas that Mr. Ramaswamy espoused, such as consolidating state universities or phasing out the state income tax completely. But it apparently appealed to voters just trying to afford daily necessities.

Dr. Acton’s personal story also seemed to resonate with voters. She was homeless for a period in her childhood, but after her mother lost custody, she found some stability living with her biological father. She entered an accelerated medical school program straight out of high school, and went on to a career in public health, with a focus on children’s health.

In 2019, Gov. Mike DeWine, a Republican, appointed Dr. Acton as director of the Ohio Department of Health. In January, she will succeed him.

item.title: Becerra Becomes California’s First Latino Elected as Governor
item.description:
Xavier Becerra, a Democrat and former Biden administration official, began the race for California governor with poll numbers so low that his own party chairman urged him to drop out.

Now, Mr. Becerra will become the next governor of the nation’s most populous state, The Associated Press said on Tuesday, a rise that was considered improbable a year ago. Mr. Becerra, 68, is the first Latino elected as governor of California, a milestone that punctuates a decades-long demographic shift in the state.

In California, many election outcomes remain unknown for days, but Mr. Becerra had so large an advantage that his win was called immediately after polls closed on Tuesday. Mr. Becerra will succeed Gov. Gavin Newsom, a fellow Democrat who could not run again because of term limits.

Mr. Becerra is likely to continue Mr. Newsom’s battles with President Trump, and he often referred during the campaign to the 122 lawsuits he filed against the first Trump administration when he was California’s attorney general. But with his mild-mannered demeanor, Mr. Becerra is expected to be less fiery than Mr. Newsom.

Mr. Becerra is likely to govern as an establishment Democrat, having won the backing of major labor unions, industry groups and the California Chamber of Commerce. He refrained from making many detailed promises during the campaign and instead sold voters on his long résumé of government experience, including his four-year tenure as state attorney general and more than two decades as a congressman.

Mr. Becerra also benefited from voters’ overwhelming disapproval of Mr. Trump in a state where registered Democrats outnumber Republicans by a roughly two-to-one margin. Mr. Becerra defeated Steve Hilton, a Republican and former Fox News host, who had what Mr. Trump called his “COMPLETE & TOTAL ENDORSEMENT.”

The president’s support helped Mr. Hilton in the primary but doomed him in the general election. California voters have not elected a Republican to statewide office in 20 years, and Mr. Trump’s relentless attacks on the state, which included deploying Marines to the streets of Los Angeles last year in response to immigration crackdown protests, have made him particularly unpopular.

Mr. Hilton tried to appeal to anti-Trump voters by focusing on California’s high cost of living in his general election campaign, arguing that conditions would only improve with a partisan change in the state’s political leadership.

Mr. Hilton’s closing argument to voters wary of the G.O.P. was to “just try it.” He spread that message with ads that played on sexual innuendo and spoofed Californians as sage-burning hippies and Hollywood hangers-on who would like Republican policies if only they’d give Mr. Hilton a try.

Mr. Hilton, 57, grew up in England and moved to California in 2012 for his wife’s career in Silicon Valley. He ran an energetic campaign and proposed lowering gas prices, building more houses and creating an Office of Fun and Freedom “to cut the killjoy rules crushing nightlife.”

Mr. Becerra will become California’s first Latino governor elected by voters but not the state’s first Latino governor. Romualdo Pacheco had that honor when he rose to the role by succession in 1875. Mr. Becerra routinely talked about his family’s Mexican roots as he campaigned in both English and Spanish this year.

His mother was from Mexico. His father was born in Sacramento and raised in Mexico. They came to California as a young couple and raised their children in Sacramento.

Mr. Hilton repeatedly attacked Mr. Becerra over his work as President Joseph R. Biden Jr.’s secretary of health and human services. The agency was responsible for helping migrant children who entered the United States without their parents. A New York Times investigation in 2023 found that many of those children wound up trafficked into dangerous jobs.

Mr. Becerra said that children were not exploited when they were under the supervision of his agency and that he was not responsible for what happened after they were released.

item.title: Talarico Wins Texas Senate Race, Ending a Three-Decade Drought for Democrats
item.description:
James Talarico, a 37-year-old Democratic state legislator, has won the race to become the next senator from Texas, The Associated Press said on Tuesday. He defeated a scandal-plagued Republican to end a three-decade drought for Democrats in one of the nation’s largest states.

The victory immediately vaulted Mr. Talarico into the political stratosphere as one of the Democratic Party’s biggest stars after he accomplished the generational dream of turning Texas blue.

Mr. Talarico toppled Ken Paxton, the Republican state attorney general and a close ally of President Trump, after a bruising and costly campaign. Mr. Talarico survived an onslaught of advertising financed by the world’s richest man, Elon Musk, who poured about $200 million into various efforts to keep the Texas seat in Republican hands.

Mr. Trump and Vice President JD Vance campaigned repeatedly for Mr. Paxton in a state that the president coasted to victory in just two years ago. Mr. Trump tried calling Mr. Talarico “Talafreako” and cast him as outside the mainstream.

But it was not enough to save Mr. Paxton.

Mr. Talarico, a Presbyterian seminarian, ran on a platform that sought to redefine the traditional divides in America as not “left versus right” but rather “top versus bottom.” And he used Mr. Musk’s unprecedented gusher of spending to further his own case as a disrupter of a broken status quo.

Democrats on pace to win large House majority

Democrats are likely to have a Senate majority of four or more seats. They won, or are favored to win, virtually every Senate battleground state.

Very likely Dem.

>95% chance of control

Mr. Paxton, 63, beat the state’s current Republican senator, John Cornyn, this spring after a prolonged primary fight by mobilizing the party’s still-potent MAGA base. Mr. Paxton had spent years courting Mr. Trump, including amplifying the president’s false claims that the 2020 election was stolen.

Republican officials, including Mr. Cornyn, had warned loudly that nominating Mr. Paxton would jeopardize the seat because of his laundry list of scandals and vulnerabilities. Mr. Trump ignored them and backed Mr. Paxton in his runoff against Mr. Cornyn anyway.

Mr. Paxton’s history of controversy is long.

He was once indicted on felony charges of securities fraud. His wife has accused him of infidelity. And he was impeached three years ago — with the support of numerous Texas Republican lawmakers — on accusations of bribery and abusing his office, though he was ultimately acquitted by the State Senate.

Mr. Talarico called Mr. Paxton “the most corrupt politician in America” and barnstormed the state with a Christianity-infused message of bipartisanship and bringing the state together. He pushed for term limits and banning congressional stock trading, and against corruption in general. He captured the imaginations of small Democratic donors online, putting him on track to raise well more than $150 million, more than any other Democrat in the 2026 midterms.

An eighth-generation Texan, Mr. Talarico campaigned on his deep ties to the state, telling the story of his mother, who left his abusive father when he was young. He first won election to the state House of Representatives in 2018, but his district was redrawn by Republicans. He eventually switched to a safer seat that now includes the liberal stronghold of Austin.

Mr. Talarico burst into view nationally in the summer of 2025 following an appearance on Joe Rogan’s podcast, with Mr. Rogan telling him at one point that he should “run for president.” Then, when Texas legislative Democrats fled the state by plane to try to forestall a Republican effort to redraw the state’s congressional lines, Mr. Talarico became a fixture on cable news programs, showcasing his media savvy.

In the primary, those skills would help him to outlast the 2024 Senate nominee, Colin Allred, who dropped out, and defeat Representative Jasmine Crockett, a Dallas Democrat and one of the party’s social media stars in her own right.

The general election was brutal. Mr. Musk’s money funded a barrage of ads. By the end of the race, the PAC funded by Mr. Musk had paid for all six of the most expensive political ads in the country this election, according to AdImpact, the advertising tracking firm.

Many slammed Mr. Talarico for his past support for transgender rights. Mr. Talarico tried to push back. “I don’t support sex change surgeries for kids,” he said in one ad of his own.

By the fall, advertising in Texas became so prohibitively expensive and the airwaves so cluttered that some groups began airing commercials nationally during football games rather than booking ads in each of the state’s many, pricey media markets.

Mr. Talarico and Mr. Paxton never debated, even as Mr. Trump called for such a face-off.

Mr. Trump campaigned repeatedly for Mr. Paxton but also commented cuttingly on his looks, including at the Republicans’ rare midterm convention, which was held in Dallas.

“I don’t like the way Ken dresses,” Mr. Trump said at one point. “I don’t really like the way Ken talks,” he said at another, before calling him the “greatest” state attorney general in the country.

Yet Republicans never fully united after the bitter primary, with Mr. Cornyn notably never endorsing Mr. Paxton even as he raised money for other Senate Republican candidates. He instead criticized Mr. Paxton’s skills and work ethic.

Mr. Talarico become the first Democrat to win statewide since 1994 — the same year that George W. Bush, the future president, won the governorship — and the first Democrat to win a Senate seat since former Lloyd Bentsen in 1988.

item.title: Alabama Democrat Holds House Seat Despite Republican Redistricting
item.description:
Alabama Republicans delayed four of the state’s congressional primaries in the spring and scrambled to implement district lines that favored conservatives in an effort to oust Representative Shomari Figures, a Democrat.

On Tuesday, Mr. Figures won re-election anyway, The Associated Press said, defeating Rhett Marques, a Republican state representative backed by President Trump.

Mr. Figures won the Second Congressional District in 2024, after a federal court said Alabama had illegally diluted the power of Black voters through gerrymandering.

When he joined Representative Terri Sewell, a Democrat, in Washington, it was the first time the state had two Black representatives in Congress at the same time in Congress.

But earlier this year, the Supreme Court effectively gave Republican lawmakers the opportunity take back the district, with a ruling that said another Southern state, Louisiana, had illegally considered race when drawing its congressional maps.

That opened the possibility for Alabama to return to a map that the federal court had thrown out under the Voting Rights Act. The Supreme Court allowed that Alabama map to take effect.

Mr. Figures was seen as the more vulnerable of the two Democrats, and Republicans redrew his district to combine the city of Montgomery, which has a majority of Black residents, with parts of a more conservative, whiter region in the district, replacing rural counties known as the Black Belt.

Mr. Marques campaigned on his alignment with President Trump and the core issues of the Republican Party. But Mr. Figures had some recognition from his two years in the House, and worked to highlight federal funds that he had directed toward the state.

He also tapped into backlash among Black voters over the new district lines, as well as frustration with Trump policies, including cuts to health care and food assistance programs.

item.title: Missouri Voters Reject Congressional Map Redrawn to Boost Republicans
item.description:
Missouri voters shot down a gerrymandered congressional map that Republicans redrew last year at President Trump’s request, The Associated Press said on Tuesday, leaving in place two districts where Democrats have an advantage.

Republican officials fought for more than a year to use the redrawn map, which would have positioned their party to flip a Democratic-held seat in the Kansas City area. But residents opposed to that switch collected hundreds of thousands of signatures seeking to put the issue to a vote, and the courts rejected a Republican attempt to exclude the question from the ballot.

The vote on Tuesday left Missouri with two solidly Democratic districts, five solidly Republican districts and one Republican-leaning district. Those boundaries, which were drawn after the 2020 census, were used in the general election on Tuesday.

But because Missouri used the redrawn map in its primary election in August, many voters did not have a voice in choosing their congressional nominees. Officials in both parties have speculated that candidates who lose the general election might challenge the results of their races in court.

Missouri was among the first states to join a national push last year to redistrict outside the usual once-a-decade cycle. Missouri Republicans, who have large legislative majorities, brushed aside Democratic objections and met in a special session to pass the new map. Representative Emanuel Cleaver, a long-serving Kansas City Democrat, was drawn into a new Republican-leaning district that stretched far into the state’s conservative countryside.

While other states, both Republican- and Democratic-led, also moved to redistrict, Missouri became unique as a dispute over which boundaries were in effect stretched past the primary election.

After redistricting opponents submitted signatures seeking a referendum on the map, Secretary of State Denny Hoskins, a Republican, waited months to announce that he believed the question did not qualify for the ballot. He made that announcement on the day of the primary, his deadline under state law, as voters were casting ballots under the redrawn borders.

But the Missouri Supreme Court found that Mr. Hoskins had erred in excluding the question from the ballot, and said that the redrawn borders could not be used until and unless they were approved by voters. The state court ordered Mr. Hoskins to conduct the general election using the older boundaries, and the U.S. Supreme Court declined to intervene when state officials appealed.

The landscape was muddied further when a federal district judge entered a conflicting order, touching off more litigation and repeated trips to the U.S. Supreme Court as deadlines to print general election ballots loomed. Republican state officials ultimately relented and instructed local officials to use the older district boundaries in November.

item.title: Paul Pelosi Prohibited From Driving After Crash in Napa Valley
item.description:
Paul Pelosi, husband of former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi, will be prohibited from driving for six months after he was convicted of crashing into a parked car over the summer, prosecutors announced on Tuesday.

Mr. Pelosi, 86, pleaded no contest to a misdemeanor hit-and-run charge and to making an unlawful turn, according to the Napa County District Attorney’s office. In July, he slammed his convertible into a parked car in Yountville, Calif., a small tourist town near Napa known for its many wine tasting rooms and its Michelin-starred restaurant, the French Laundry.

As part of the plea agreement, Mr. Pelosi will be prohibited from driving for six months. He will also be placed on one year of summary probation and has been ordered to complete a 10-day work program, according to the district attorney’s office. He paid court fees as well as more than $11,000 in restitution to the owner of the car that he hit, the office said.

Mr. Pelosi has an erratic driving record that dates back years.

In 2022, he pleaded guilty to driving under the influence after crashing his Porsche into an oncoming Jeep. He has also received several traffic violations in the San Francisco Bay Area over the past 15 years, including driving the wrong way down a one-way street, speeding and, on more than one occasion, driving through a red light, court records show.

In July, Mr. Pelosi was about 15 minutes from the Pelosis’ Napa Valley estate when he hit a parked Tesla. He then continued driving down a residential street in Napa Valley until his car broke down and law enforcement officers arrived at the scene.

The Tesla was clipped so hard that the rear bumper was smashed in and one of its front wheels climbed the curb, neighbors said.

Mr. Pelosi’s attorney could not immediately be reached for comment.

item.title: Sherrod Brown Regains an Ohio Senate Seat in Crucial Win for Democrats
item.description:
Sherrod Brown, a former Democratic senator from Ohio, will represent his state again after unseating Senator Jon Husted on Tuesday, according to The Associated Press. Mr. Brown’s victory in one of the midterms’ marquee races flips a seat central to the Democrats’ quest to retake control of the Senate.

Mr. Brown, 73, will return to Washington two years after he was defeated by Senator Bernie Moreno of Ohio. His comeback reflects just how much the political environment has changed since the Republican Party swept into power in 2024.

It is also a significant blow to President Trump and the Republican Party, which invested more time and resources into this race than all but one other contest during the most expensive election cycle in modern history.

Ohio backed Mr. Trump in all three of his presidential bids, serving as a cornerstone of his political rise.

Mr. Husted was appointed to the Senate in 2025 to finish the term of Mr. Trump’s current vice president, JD Vance. He ran as a business-minded conservative closely aligned with the White House, diverging from other battleground candidates who distanced themselves from the president as his popularity sagged.

Despite the time he had spent as the state’s lieutenant governor, Mr. Husted struggled to introduce himself to voters. Some in the state believed Mr. Brown, a fixture in Ohio politics since the 1970s, was the incumbent in the race.

As much as the results reflected the weaknesses of Mr. Husted and his party, they revealed the strengths of Mr. Brown for this particular political moment.

More comfortable in a fleece than a suit, Mr. Brown has spent the better part of five decades preaching a version of economic populism that calls the system in Washington rigged and frames policy disputes as battles between workers and billionaires.

That proved to be the message that voters, focused on affordability and wary of corruption, wanted to hear.

Mr. Brown ran a campaign respected by even Republican operatives in Ohio. He was early to recognize widespread concern about data centers, and he made Mr. Husted a target by running ads that called out his support of such investments when he served in state government.

His victory marks a triumph not only over Mr. Husted but also over the cryptocurrency industry, whose main super PAC, Fairshake, spent $41 million to help oust Mr. Brown two years ago.

item.title: Rob Sand Is Elected Iowa Governor, Ending Republicans’ Hold on the Seat
item.description:
Rob Sand, the Iowa state auditor who ran as a Democrat fed up with partisan politics, won the race for governor on Tuesday, defeating Zach Lahn, a Republican, according to The Associated Press.

The win ended a nearly 16-year stretch of Republicans’ occupying the governor’s mansion in Des Moines — a sign that the grip of conservative control in once deep-red Iowa has weakened.

Mr. Sand, 44, won over Iowans with a pragmatic pitch: He was a former prosecutor practiced at rooting out fraud who would work closely with Republicans if elected.

The rest of his biography was also an unconventional mix. A churchgoing Ivy League graduate from a small town in northeast Iowa, he drove a Ford pickup truck and talked on the campaign trail about his passion for hunting and fishing. Rows of taxidermied deer heads hang in his office at the State Capitol.

He will still face a wall of opposition in the Republican-controlled State Legislature. For years, Republicans have dominated both chambers of the Legislature and filled all six of the state’s seats in Congress. President Trump won Iowa in 2024 by more than 13 percentage points.

But Mr. Sand’s ascendance suggests that Mr. Trump’s popularity has sunk and that Iowans are fed up with the direction of their state.

At campaign rallies and town halls, voters said that they were frustrated by the high price of gas, groceries and housing, blaming not just their state leadership, but also the Republican Party. Farmers in this agriculture-heavy state have been furious about tariffs, trade wars and diesel costs, and Iowans in rural areas and cities said they were alarmed by the rising cancer rates that made the state an outlier.

Mr. Sand, a longtime Democrat, made a pitch to voters that he was not a typical partisan. He repeated the campaign slogan, “Not redder or bluer, but better and truer,” and promised to be a “governor for all.” His campaign signs explicitly avoided the usual Democratic blue, instead designed in shades of forest green and blaze orange that nodded to Iowa’s hunting tradition.

“I think one of the biggest problems that we have right now is that the Democratic and Republican parties basically are functioning like two private clubs,” Mr. Sand said. “They’re more interested in beating up on each other and in following their leaders for the most part than they are in actually serving the people that elect them. And you can see that pretty clearly in Iowa.”

Mr. Sand ran unopposed in the Democratic primary. In the general election, he faced Mr. Lahn, who lives on his family farm in Belle Plaine, Iowa, but who also spends significant time in Wichita, Kan. Mr. Lahn answered accusations that he was only a part-time Iowa resident by saying that he and his wife travel to Wichita to spend time with their children in their blended family.

But the carpetbagger label stuck, and Mr. Lahn struggled to break through with moderate Republicans.

item.title: Democrat Wins Race for Texas Governor in Tectonic Upset
item.description:
State Representative Gina Hinojosa pulled off a seismic upset in the race for Texas governor, The Associated Press said Tuesday, denying the state’s Republican governor, Greg Abbott, a record-setting fourth term and making history as the first Hispanic to be elected to lead the state.

She also became one of the first Democrats to win statewide office in more than 30 years.

Ms. Hinojosa, 52, ended more than a generation of one-party rule in Texas, defeating a well-funded incumbent once seen as unbeatable.

The mood at her election night party at Assembly Hall in Austin, Texas, became electric almost as soon as the results started coming in. Many Latinas in the room became emotional when it became clear that she would become the first Hispanic governor in Texas, a state where Latinos make up the largest population in the United States.

Hundreds of people cheered and applauded each time the television screens showed the sitting governor, Greg Abbott, trailing her.

While much of the attention — and money — in Texas this midterm election season went to the state’s heated Senate campaign, Ms. Hinojosa emerged late in the year as a potential winner after polls shifted in her favor.

During his decade as governor, Mr. Abbott became one of the most powerful men to serve in that role, using executive orders and key appointments to strengthen his control over state operations. He drew on the connections and experience he gained as attorney general and as a justice on the Texas Supreme Court.

Ms. Hinojosa, who had never served in statewide office, brought his decades in public service to an abrupt and unexpected halt.

A civil rights and labor lawyer, Ms. Hinojosa has spent nearly a decade in the statehouse, representing a solidly Democratic district in Austin.

She only entered the race when no other Democrat would, part of her party’s push to field a candidate in every race in the state. But the headwinds facing the Republicans nationally became a wind at her back.

Like many competitive elections this year, the race for governor of Texas became a referendum on affordability.

Mr. Abbott made Ms. Hinojosa’s liberal legislative record a point of attack. In ads, paid for with Mr. Abbott’s massive campaign war chest, he brought up her past support for transgender rights and opposition to enshrining the state’s income tax ban in the Texas Constitution, which Mr. Abbott argued was akin to a vote for tax increases.

Ms. Hinojosa criticized Mr. Abbott over his past support for the state’s proliferating data centers, and made the argument that Republicans, who have controlled every branch of state government for more than 20 years, were not putting everyday Texans and their needs first.

As the state’s first Democratic governor since Ann Richards left office in 1995, Ms. Hinojosa will have to expend significant energy unwinding the many threads of power woven into place by Republicans during their decades in power. That task could be made easier if Democrats manage to wrest control of the Legislature from Republicans.

item.title: Missouri Voters Reject Republican Attempt to Restore Ban on Abortions
item.description:
Republican legislators in Missouri, disappointed by voters’ decision to add abortion rights to the State Constitution two years ago, asked them to reconsider on Tuesday. The result was the same, with Missourians rejecting the attempt to largely outlaw the procedure, The Associated Press said.

The vote demonstrated again how the politics of abortion have shifted since the Supreme Court overturned Roe v. Wade in 2022, with residents of conservative states often supporting abortion rights against the wishes of their elected leaders. Voters in Kansas, Montana and Ohio, among other states, have also opted to keep or establish abortion rights since that ruling.

Missouri officials swiftly enacted a ban on nearly all abortions after the Supreme Court decision, but had to reverse course after voters narrowly approved a constitutional right to abortion in 2024.

Months after that vote, Republicans reopened the debate and placed a question on this year’s ballot asking voters to ban abortion in nearly all cases. The new ban would have included exceptions for medical emergencies and for cases of rape or incest if the assault was reported to the police within 48 hours and the pregnancy was less than 12 weeks along. Some Republicans had opposed the rape and incest exceptions.

The ballot question on Tuesday also included language that would have added a ban on gender transition treatments for minors to the Missouri Constitution.

Republicans hold large legislative majorities in Missouri, and the party wins statewide elections in blowouts. But the state’s voters have repeatedly frustrated Republican officials by enacting left-leaning policy goals through ballot questions, including by expanding Medicaid and legalizing marijuana and sports betting. In August, voters overwhelmingly rejected an attempt to make it harder to amend the State Constitution.

item.title: Democrat Wins a Kansas Senate Seat for the First Time Since 1932
item.description:
The Rev. Adam Hamilton on Tuesday became the first Democrat to win a Senate seat in Kansas since the Great Depression, according to The Associated Press, stunning Senator Roger Marshall, a one-term Republican.

Mr. Hamilton, a centrist from the Kansas City area who was registered as a Republican until February, rode voters’ frustration with the economy and disenchantment with Mr. Marshall to the upset victory. Mr. Marshall had campaigned with President Trump in the final days of the race and received late financial support from the national Republican Party, but it was not enough.

Mr. Hamilton, in capping his pulpit-to-politics journey, became the first Democrat to win a Senate race in Kansas since 1932.

There had been subtle signs in recent years that Kansas was shifting to the left, electing a Democratic governor for two terms and a gay Native American Democrat to Congress in 2018.

And signs of discontent with Mr. Marshall appeared as early as March 2025, when he had to abruptly end a town hall-style meeting and walk out because voters were so angry with him.

Still, Mr. Trump carried Kansas by 16 points in 2024, and the race was not initially expected to be competitive. Both parties started to focus more on it in the early fall after opinion polls showed the candidates in a dead heat.

Democrats on pace to win large House majority

Democrats are likely to have a Senate majority of four or more seats. They won, or are favored to win, virtually every Senate battleground state.

Very likely Dem.

>95% chance of control

Mr. Marshall found himself on the defensive after a New York Times report that he had filed lawsuits against more than 700 patients with outstanding bills during his decades-long career as an obstetrician-gynecologist and routinely charged patients an 18 percent annual interest rate. In the final days of the race, a former patient of Mr. Marshall’s filed a class-action lawsuit against him and his former medical practice, accusing him of charging illegally high interest rates as he pursued patients over unpaid bills.

And late in the campaign, Mr. Marshall went rogue, filming an ad in which he attributed his past debt collection efforts to a need to “keep the lights on.” After shooting the spot against the advice of his aides, he began to send the video around, and it eventually landed on social media the Saturday before the election.

His campaign also contended with an ethics complaint in October from a watchdog group claiming that he had illegally used taxpayer funds to pay campaign staff, and a late-race revelation that he had an unpaid bakery bill of $678.75 from his primary night watch party in 2020. (Mr. Marshall subsequently paid the bill with interest.)

Mr. Hamilton, the founder of the 24,000-member Church of the Resurrection, the largest church in Kansas and the nation’s largest United Methodist congregation, also had particular strengths.

He presented as a sure-footed centrist with decades of experience working crowds. He proved to be a strong fund-raiser. And before he made a single campaign promise, many in Kansas were familiar with him from TV broadcasts of his church services.

Recruited by the Kansas Democratic Party after considering an independent run, Mr. Hamilton argued that Mr. Marshall was siding with Mr. Trump over Kansas. The race played out as challenges piled up for farmers in the deeply Republican and heavily agricultural state.

Ranchers there are contending with high costs of diesel, gasoline and fertilizer because of the war in Iran, policies that sent a flood of beef imports into the United States with lower levies and an immigration crackdown that limited the number of farm workers.

As Election Day approached, Kansas was also dealing with a drought, hampering yields of soybeans, wheat and corn and intensifying farmers’ misery. The approval rating of Mr. Trump, who won Kansas by double digits in three straight presidential elections, slipped well underwater in the state by this fall, according to polls.

Mr. Marshall sought to fend off Mr. Hamilton by arguing that the Democrat was a novice who would be beholden to party leaders, such as Senator Chuck Schumer of New York.

Mr. Hamilton parried those attacks by vowing to oppose Mr. Schumer’s bid to become majority leader should Democrats win the Senate, and by casting himself as a cooperative, independent-minded lawmaker comfortable working with Republicans.

He described former President Joseph R. Biden Jr.’s immigration policies as a “disaster” and denounced the growth in the national debt.

Mr. Hamilton had received some valuable endorsements. Two Republican former Kansas governors, Bill Graves and Mike Hayden, backed him. Arch Naramore, a centrist Republican who won a fifth of the vote in the Republican Senate primary, supported Mr. Hamilton, saying that Mr. Marshall was a “sycophant” for Mr. Trump.

And former Senator Sheila Frahm of Kansas, a Republican who served briefly in Senator Bob Dole’s seat after he resigned in 1996, endorsed Mr. Hamilton, too. She had supported Mr. Marshall in 2020.

“I was excited about his candidacy,” Ms. Frahm said in an interview, referring to Mr. Marshall. “And really it’s been hard to say that we’ve even seen him since.”

And like many others in Kansas, she said she had known Mr. Hamilton for years and that she felt he could work with “all kinds of people.” But ultimately Kansas voters were venting frustration with economic conditions, Ms. Frahm said.

“We’re just unhappy,” she said.

The last Democrat to win a Senate race in Kansas was George S. McGill. He narrowly defeated a Republican in 1932, as deep dissatisfaction with President Herbert Hoover’s handling of the Great Depression powered Democratic gains across the country and sent Franklin Delano Roosevelt to the White House.

Senator McGill was defeated by 12 points in 1938.

item.title: Wisconsin Elects Its First Black Governor, a Democrat
item.description:
David Crowley, the Milwaukee County executive, defeated Representative Tom Tiffany in the race for Wisconsin governor on Tuesday, according to The Associated Press. He will become the first Black governor in state history.

Mr. Crowley, 40, began his run for governor as a near-unknown who barely registered in the polls, trailing near the back of the Democratic pack. But after an endorsement from Gov. Tony Evers, he catapulted over a buzzy democratic socialist in the primary. In the general election he beat a sitting congressman who is closely aligned with President Trump.

His victory keeps the governor’s mansion in Democratic hands and gives the party a shot at winning a trifecta if they flip both chambers of the State Legislature from Republican control.

Wisconsin is known for its razor-thin margins in statewide races, with nearly equal numbers of registered Democrats and Republicans. Voters have been bombarded with mailers, robocalls and television ads from Mr. Tiffany and Mr. Crowley. Mr. Tiffany played up his small-town roots, his upbringing on a dairy farm and his background working as a dam tender and owner of a river cruise business. During the one and only television debate between Mr. Tiffany and Mr. Crowley, Mr. Tiffany vowed that he would never allow a data center to be built “on our beautiful farmland here in Wisconsin.”

Mr. Tiffany is known as one of the most conservative members of Congress. He is part of the Freedom Caucus, a small but influential group of House representatives who have pushed the Republican agenda further to the right.

Mr. Crowley highlighted his own biography as a child of Milwaukee, the biggest city in the state. He experienced poverty growing up on the North Side with working-class parents who used drugs and were evicted during the city’s crack cocaine epidemic.

He has served as the Milwaukee County executive since 2020. He is known as a pragmatist and moderate Democrat who cut county property taxes and frequently worked with Republicans to strike bipartisan deals.

Mr. Crowley promised that as governor he would focus on improving life for Wisconsin’s working people, expand public health care and affordable housing, and invest more money in the state’s public education system.

And he warned voters that they could not trust Mr. Tiffany, describing him as an out-of-touch MAGA conservative whose campaign was largely funded by billionaires.

“He went to Washington, and he sold Wisconsin out,” Mr. Crowley said during a debate in October. “He went to go work for Donald Trump and the billionaires bankrolling him. They got tax breaks, you got higher bills. They got tariffs, you got higher prices. They got their endless war, you got record high gas prices.”

Mr. Tiffany tried to distance himself from Mr. Trump, dodging questions about his ties to the president, but in the end was unable to convince enough moderate Republicans and independents to vote for him.

item.title: Josh Turek Flips Iowa Senate Seat in a Major Victory for Democrats
item.description:
Josh Turek, a Paralympian and Democratic state representative, flipped Iowa’s open Senate seat on Tuesday, according to The Associated Press. He overcame Representative Ashley Hinson, a third-term Republican, in one of this year’s top battleground races.

Mr. Turek’s victory, projected earlier by The New York Times, came in a state that President Trump won three times, including by 13 percentage points in 2024. It delivers Democrats a seat viewed as crucial to the party’s fight for control of the Senate and signals a backlash to President Trump’s policies in America’s heartland.

Mr. Turek campaigned hard against the president’s tariffs and the war in Iran, argued that Ms. Hinson’s alignment with Mr. Trump was hurting Iowans and slammed her for supporting cuts to Medicaid and food stamps. He also cast her as out of touch, emphasizing her personal wealth and her votes in favor of tax breaks that benefited the upper class.

The political environment worked in Mr. Turek’s favor as farmers struggled with the high costs of fertilizer, diesel and gas because of Mr. Trump’s tariffs and the war.

Mr. Turek also eschewed his party’s less popular positions, saying in a campaign ad that he would work with “anyone,” including Mr. Trump, to secure the border and steering clear of culture war issues on the trail. He had a history of seeking out bipartisanship: He flipped his Republican-leaning Iowa House district by six votes in 2022 and is among the few Democrats elected in Western Iowa, a conservative area.

Ms. Hinson’s loss is a blow to the state’s Republican establishment. She entered the race with stronger name recognition than Mr. Turek, having worked as a television journalist in Cedar Rapids for a decade before becoming a state representative, then a congresswoman. She was viewed as a top recruit for Republicans.

Ms. Hinson sought to escape Mr. Trump’s flagging approval rating in Iowa by criticizing some of his executive orders, including a move to reduce tariffs on some foreign ground beef that Midwestern ranchers vehemently opposed. But she also kept his base close, rallying with Mr. Trump in Sioux City two weeks before the election. In the end, her longtime support for the president’s agenda was difficult for her to overcome.

Mr. Turek’s victory is likely to set off worries among Iowa Republicans ahead of the 2028 presidential election. Former President Barack Obama twice won the state before Mr. Trump flipped it in 2016.

Supporters said Mr. Turek’s life story inspired them. A two-time Paralympic gold medalist in basketball, he uses a wheelchair because he was born with spina bifida, a condition connected to his father’s exposure to Agent Orange in the Vietnam War.

When Mr. Turek is sworn in next year, he will succeed Senator Joni Ernst, a Republican who declined to seek re-election.

And he will inherit the seat once held by former Senator Tom Harkin, a Democrat whose legacy rests on his passage of the Americans With Disabilities Act, a landmark civil rights law for people with disabilities. At a campaign event two weeks ago, Mr. Turek said it would be “poetic” for him to win the seat.

“I’m only here because of the work of Senator Harkin,” he said.

item.title: Winning the Senate, Democrats Secure a Platform to Check Trump
item.description:
Democrats seized control of the Senate on Tuesday, according to New York Times projections, capturing a powerful platform to counter President Trump as voters in Republican-leaning states repudiated the president and his allies in a midterm thrashing.

Democrats clinched the Senate majority with a win in Iowa and were picking up competitive House seats around the country that pointed to a lopsided margin of control in that chamber.

The results promised a new era of divided government in Washington and a freshly assertive Congress after two years in which Republicans generally ceded power to Mr. Trump and reduced the legislative branch’s role to that of a mere bystander.

They sealed a volatile election season that began with Democrats having little chance of taking over the Senate or cutting very deeply into Republicans’ 53-to-47 majority.

But over the past year, the electorate soured on Mr. Trump, and Democrats even in Republican-leaning states romped to victory, picking up support in even traditionally conservative strongholds by capitalizing on mounting unrest over the war with Iran and its consequences. With fuel prices soaring and tariffs exacerbating already high living costs, they made the case that Republicans in Washington were cashing in while ordinary Americans were struggling.

Democrats on pace to win large House majority

Democrats are likely to have a Senate majority of four or more seats. They won, or are favored to win, virtually every Senate battleground state.

Dem. control

Very likely Dem.

>95% chance of control

“We listened to the American people, what they wanted,” Senator Chuck Schumer of New York, the Democratic leader, said late Tuesday night during a news conference in Washington. “We listened, they didn’t. And the American people reduced the red brick wall to a pile of bricks.”

The result was that Democrats were able to reshape a political map that was stacked against them with seats in solidly Republican territory, flipping seats in Kansas, Texas, Ohio, and both North and South Carolina.

They held onto a pair of seats in New Hampshire and Georgia that Republicans had once hoped to flip to help offset losses elsewhere that became increasingly out of reach for the G.OP. amid rising discontent over Mr. Trump’s policies.

Democratic control of the Senate as of Jan. 3 will give the party veto power over Mr. Trump’s judicial and administration nominees, as well as the leadership of the committees that will have the authority to subpoena administration officials and others to follow through on investigations Democrats promised to pursue if they won.

It will also give Democrats control of the Senate floor and legislative agenda, setting up likely clashes with the White House over spending, the war with Iran and a host of special projects that the president has undertaken around Washington. The loss could spur Republicans in the coming weeks to try to push through some of their priorities in a catchall bill in an upcoming lame-duck session that begins on Monday.

The outcome represents a stunning defeat for Senate Republicans who began the midterm cycle with substantial advantages but saw them eroded by the actions of the president and their unwillingness to push back on Mr. Trump.

The possibility that Democrats could be in position to win the Senate majority was almost unthinkable a year ago. The playing field was clearly tilted in favor of Senate Republicans defending seats in G.O.P.-leaning states, and Democrats faced a challenge in retaining the 47 seats they controlled. But economic conditions and the president’s decision to initiate a costly conflict with Iran in February opened the door for Democrats.

With legislative accomplishments hard to come by, Republicans were counting on an electoral reward from the “big beautiful bill” passed under a special party-line process and signed into law by Mr. Trump in July 2025 after Vice President JD Vance was forced to break a tie vote. The measure extended income tax cuts secured by Republicans during Mr. Trump’s first term and also instituted some new breaks such as easing taxes on tips and increasing the deduction for state and local taxes.

Their opponents, however, assailed the legislation’s cuts in safety net programs and a G.O.P. refusal to extend some subsidies for the Affordable Care Act. Democrats began building a case that Republican policies were making life more unaffordable while Mr. Trump and the people surrounding him were reaping huge financial benefits.

Tariffs imposed by the president helped bolster that argument, with his trade war with Canada hitting particularly hard in Michigan and Maine, two states where Republicans hoped to win to counter potential Democratic wins elsewhere. The tariffs also drove up farm fertilizer costs and dried up commodity markets, hitting conservative voters in the agriculture states.

Then the war with Iran strangled fuel supplies, sharply driving up the price of regular gasoline and diesel fuel while frustrating voters who backed Mr. Trump for his pledges to stay out of overseas conflicts.

The president’s attacks on some in his own party also created targets of opportunity for Democrats. After Senator Thom Tillis, Republican of North Carolina, voted against advancing the “big beautiful bill” in June 2025, Mr. Trump laid into him. Mr. Tillis responded by announcing he would not seek re-election, putting that state’s Senate seat in play. Former Gov. Roy Cooper won the seat on Tuesday.

In Texas, Mr. Trump gave a last-minute endorsement to Ken Paxton over Senator John Cornyn, the Republican incumbent, in the state primary, appearing to help lift Mr. Paxton to the win. With Mr. Paxton on the ballot, Democrats rallied behind Mr. Talarico, turning Texas, where a Democrat had not been elected to the Senate since 1988, into one of the nation’s fiercest races, forcing Republicans to invest tens of millions of dollars there.

Many analysts said in the lead-up to the election that Mr. Cornyn, in contrast, would have had a fairly easy time holding off Mr. Talarico in the general election. But Mr. Trump held a grudge from when Mr. Cornyn in 2023 suggested misgivings about the president seeking a second term despite Mr. Cornyn’s generally supportive record. Mr. Trump ended up backing Mr. Paxton despite the political risks.

Robert Jimison contributed reporting from Washington.

item.title: Luria Wins in Virginia, Flipping a Key House Seat for Democrats

item.title: Peggy Flanagan’s Victory Keeps Minnesota Senate Seat in Democratic Hands
item.description:
Peggy Flanagan, a Democrat who has served two terms as Minnesota’s lieutenant governor, defeated the former sports broadcaster Michele Tafoya, according to The Associated Press. The contest to replace the retiring Senator Tina Smith became surprisingly competitive in the final weeks.

Ms. Flanagan, who has governed Minnesota alongside Gov. Tim Walz, since 2019, made history as the first Native American woman elected to the Senate.

She ran on an unabashedly liberal agenda, vowing to fight for the universal health care policy known as Medicare for All, pursue a sweeping overhaul of the immigration enforcement system and set a $17 federal minimum wage.

As she campaigned, Ms. Flanagan, 47, faced questions about her role in a scandal over widespread fraud in state-run safety net programs.

Prosecutors and lawmakers from both parties said that the Walz administration was slow to respond to brazen schemes that resulted in the theft of hundreds of millions of dollars from programs meant to feed low-income children, treat minors with autism and help people at risk of homelessness.

That was a dominant issue during the primary race, in which Ms. Flanagan trounced a centrist rival, Representative Angie Craig. And it was the main line of attack in Ms. Tafoya’s bid to win a Senate seat in a state that hasn’t elected a Republican senator since 2002.

Ms. Flanagan sought to deflect responsibility for the fraud by arguing that Mr. Walz, who is leaving office, had taken the lead in responding to the problem. And she sought to portray Ms. Tafoya as beholden to President Trump and his agenda.

Ms. Flanagan criticized Ms. Tafoya’s support for the war in Iran after her opponent suggested in March that Americans forgo trips to Starbucks to compensate for the rising cost of fuel caused by the conflict.

As Democrats were bullish about winning races in traditionally Republican areas during the final weeks of the midterm campaign, polls suggested that the Minnesota Senate race was close.

Political observers attributed that in part to Ms. Tafoya’s relatively moderate stances on issues such as abortion rights and the deep frustration among Minnesotans about rising taxes and fraud.

item.title: Democrat Unseats House Republican in Iowa, Flipping an Important Seat
item.description:
Christina Bohannan, a Democrat and former state legislator, defeated Representative Mariannette Miller-Meeks of Iowa, according to The Associated Press, flipping a critical Republican-held seat and delivering a significant victory for Democrats in their bid to win control of the House.

Ms. Bohannan’s victory represented the end of a long political battle against Ms. Miller-Meeks, a third-term Republican who had repeatedly held off Democratic challenges by narrow margins, including by just 799 votes over Ms. Bohannan in 2024.

But this year, with President Trump’s approval ratings sinking and his economic agenda increasingly unpopular, Ms. Miller-Meeks — like many Republicans across the country — faced a substantially more difficult political environment.

By the final weeks of the campaign, two of the most powerful Republican super PACs had effectively abandoned her, withdrawing millions of dollars in planned advertising as party strategists concluded that her seat in a competitive district spanning southeastern Iowa and the Quad Cities area had become increasingly difficult to defend.

Ms. Bohannan, a law professor who previously served in the Iowa Legislature, made the rising cost of living, federal health care cuts and the war with Iran central to her campaign, arguing that Ms. Miller-Meeks had consistently placed loyalty to Mr. Trump ahead of the interests of her constituents.

During their only debate, in October, Ms. Bohannan criticized the incumbent for repeatedly opposing congressional efforts to halt the war before reversing course as public opinion turned against it.

“The American people are hurting; they don’t want this war,” Ms. Bohannan said, calling Republicans in Congress “a rubber stamp the entire time.”

Ms. Miller-Meeks, a former ophthalmologist and military veteran, defended her record. She promoted the tax cuts Republicans enacted last year as part of their major domestic policy law and claimed that the deep cuts to Medicaid included in that measure would preserve benefits for those who needed them.

She also maintained that Mr. Trump’s tariffs would help bring manufacturing jobs to Iowa and said her decision to drop her opposition to a resolution to rein in Mr. Trump’s power to wage war with Iran reflected changing circumstances.

Ms. Bohannan argued that the administration’s tariffs were hurting Iowa farmers and that Republican cuts to Medicaid threatened rural hospitals already struggling to remain open.

Ms. Bohannan’s victory was especially significant given her previous defeats. Ms. Miller-Meeks beat her by roughly seven percentage points in 2022 before surviving their rematch two years later by fewer than 800 votes, one of the narrowest margins in the country.

Rather than retreat after those losses, Ms. Bohannan mounted another campaign focused on reaching voters in the district’s rural communities and smaller towns, including places that had supported Mr. Trump.

For Ms. Miller-Meeks, who had survived several exceptionally close elections, the loss means the end of a run in Congress that began with a victory by just six votes in 2020.

item.title: Two Native American Women Break Political Barriers This Election
item.description:
Two Native American women made history in the midterm elections: Deb Haaland, a New Mexico Democrat, will be the nation’s first woman Native American governor, and Peggy Flanagan, a Democrat of Minnesota, is the first Native American woman to win election to the Senate.

A third Indigenous woman, Mary Peltola, could also be elected to the Senate from Alaska, but her state’s unique ranked choice voting system ensures that a victor in that close race might not be known for days, if not weeks.

This week’s victories were the latest in a string of political accomplishments for Native women in the United States. Ms. Haaland, a member of the Laguna Pueblo, has been at the forefront of those milestones: In 2018, she was one of two Native American women elected to the U.S. House, and under the Biden administration, she was confirmed as the first Native American cabinet secretary, overseeing the Interior Department.

In that role, she helped the administration focus on tribal issues, including devoting resources toward finding missing or murdered Indigenous women and conducting a review of the government-run schools that Native children were forced to attend. It was a significant historical shift for an agency that played a large role in the oppression of the nation’s Indigenous people.

She will succeed Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham, a Democrat who is term-limited, in New Mexico.

In Minnesota, Ms. Flanagan, a member of the White Earth Band of Ojibwe, will take the seat left vacant by Senator Tina Smith, a Democrat. Ms. Flanagan, the state’s lieutenant governor, worked to improve relations between the state government and the 11 tribal nations in the state as part of her work in Minnesota government.

Ms. Peltola, a Democrat, became the first Alaska Native to serve in the House in 2022. She could double the number of Indigenous women elected to the Senate if she prevails.

item.title: ‘An Earthquake’: A Democratic Rout Stuns Texas
item.description:
Texas may never be the same.

Democrats shattered the 32-year-long Republican grip on statewide offices in what had been, until Tuesday, the nation’s most populous conservative state.

James Talarico’s victory over Ken Paxton, a scandal-scarred Republican candidate, in the U.S. Senate race was only the beginning of a series of seismic victories for Democrats on Tuesday in Texas.

Gina Hinojosa made history with her defeat of Gov. Greg Abbott, the third-term governor and political powerhouse who, just a few months ago, appeared to have a lock on winning a record fourth term. She becomes Texas's first Hispanic governor.

In one night, the state was transformed.

“Talarico is a symbol. Gina is an earthquake,” said Garry Mauro, a former Texas land commissioner who was among the last Democrats to win a statewide race, in 1994. “It’s a tsunami. The world has changed. The political maps will never be the same again.”

The decades of total Republican Party domination are over. Its hegemony had resulted in a succession of increasingly conservative leaders, from George W. Bush to Rick Perry to Greg Abbott, and increasingly conservative lawmaking, including abortion bans, Christian teaching material in public schools and expanded gun rights.

Democrats in Texas rose as national blowback against the Trump administration mounted among voters troubled by the war in Iran, an intense immigration crackdown and cost-of-living concerns. But Mr. Paxton owed much of his success to his closeness to Mr. Trump and Mr. Abbott tied himself closely to Mr. Trump’s policies.

Republican leaders in the state also embraced a data center boom that was unpopular in many rural and suburban areas and pushed through a school voucher program that many saw as undercutting public schools. In 2026, some party members made the state’s swelling South Asian community a boogeyman, warning of sharia law. A candidate for a top regulatory job attacked his opponents with slurs for gay and disabled people.

“I’ve watched Republicans fumble this ball from bottom to top,” said Austin Vaughn, 31, of Fort Bend County, who said he “literally checked every blue box for the first time in my life.”

He said he used to feel at home in the Republican Party in Texas, and even worked for a state legislator. But in recent years, the party “got really out of control socially.”

He now has a daughter and did not like the state’s stringent abortion ban. And, he said, while the party used to have a good message boosting and attracting businesses, they long ago lost that plot.

“No one can afford anything anymore,” he said. “Our water and air is the dirtiest and our education is horrible.”

Also swept away Tuesday was the assumption that Texas’s political future would resemble its past. In its place, something far less certain, more contested and decidedly Democratic emerged on Tuesday.

It was, for Democrats, so unexpected and so sudden, that many were still processing the implications.

“I’m jubilant,” Rafael Anchía, a Democratic state representative from the Dallas area, said as he watched the returns at Mr. Talarico’s election night party in Austin. “This is exceeding my wildest expectations.”

Mr. Anchía said that Democrats had racked up big gains all over the state, even in formerly conservative suburbs, even in rural areas where they had not competed for years: “It’s a nuke.”

The magnitude of the Democratic wave was amplified by the remarkable spectacle of Elon Musk, the world’s richest man, spending hundreds of millions of dollars in a doomed effort to preserve the state’s Republican leadership. After moving parts of his business empire to Texas, Mr. Musk poured at least $212 million into supporting Mr. Paxton, which was part of at least $224 million devoted to races in the state.

Republicans were left rattled and trying to explain not only Mr. Paxton’s spectacular loss, but how Mr. Abbott, seen as such a formidable opponent, could have been washed away as well in the national Democratic wave.

“Our party is going to have a reckoning unlike any in the history of our state,” said Matt Mackowiak, a Republican strategist who worked on Senator John Cornyn’s doomed primary campaign earlier this year against Mr. Paxton, who had been Texas’s attorney general.

As the results crystallized, Democrats believed their victory would draw more campaign money into Texas for future elections, along with greater national support. The party could seize more offices and perhaps have a shot at flipping Texas blue in a presidential election.

“You never give your enemy a beachhead; once they get it, they advance,” said Chad Wilbanks, a Republican political consultant and the former executive director of the Republican Party of Texas. “The dam is broken.”

Democratic officials said the election could also reshape state policy, ending Texas’s role as a laboratory for conservative laws nationwide. Mr. Talarico, as a U.S. senator, will not directly affect day-to-day governance in Texas. But Ms. Hinojosa will have the power to veto legislation and to appoint agency leaders.

“Texas is ready for change,” said Kendall Scudder, the chairman of the Texas Democratic Party. He said Democrats were “excited and ready to deliver on the policies that will make life more affordable” and to “root out the corruption that has plagued our politics for too long.”

President Trump crisscrossed the state, hoping he could save Mr. Paxton’s campaign in its final weeks. But his efforts at bringing Texas Republicans together against a shared Democratic enemy masked deep underlying divisions within the party.

The state’s Bush-era conservatives long opposed Mr. Paxton and his Trump-aligned wing of the party, and instead supported Mr. Cornyn in the primary. They argued that the Republican Party had drifted too far from its principles.

The two main factions of Texas Republicans have been at odds for years. Mr. Paxton often found himself at the fault line of those conflicts. His 2023 impeachment on allegations of corruption by a majority in the Texas House became a referendum on the direction of the party. His defense team argued that a faction of old-school conservatives — aligned with the Bush family and longtime Republican strategist Karl Rove — had been behind the impeachment. Republicans in the Texas Senate, overseen by Lt. Gov. Dan Patrick, an ally of Mr. Paxton, acquitted him.

Even before the vote on Tuesday, Republicans in Mr. Paxton’s camp were seething at those they saw as having supported him with insufficient vigor.

Steve Toth, a Republican candidate for the U.S. House and a Paxton ally, said those close to Mr. Cornyn and the Bush family were to blame for “dirtying” Mr. Paxton with the failed impeachment and during the Republican primary campaign.

“They never got on board,” Mr. Toth said on Monday at one of Mr. Paxton’s last campaign events, in Conroe, a city outside of Houston.

Those in Mr. Cornyn’s camp remained frustrated that Mr. Paxton had challenged him at all. Mr. Cornyn had shown little vulnerability among general election voters, even as Republican activists accused him of being insufficiently supportive of President Trump. Mr. Paxton, the hard right’s choice, easily defeated him in a primary runoff despite being vastly outspent.

Before Tuesday, the closest that Republicans in Texas had come to a statewide loss in recent years was in 2018, when Beto O’Rourke, a U.S. representative from El Paso, came within three percentage points of defeating Senator Ted Cruz. In response, Republicans in the state appeared to moderate their agenda in the next legislative session, focusing less on cultural issues and more on property tax and school financing reforms.

Now, any change in direction will involve the decisions not only of Republicans. It will involve Democrats as well.

“It’s a whole new day for Texas,” said Mr. Mauro, the former land commissioner. “After I lost in ’98, I was thinking we were one cycle away from winning to the next election. It’s been a long wait.”

Sabrina Tavernise contributed reporting.

item.title: Bobby Pulido, a Tejano Music Star, Flips a House Seat in Texas for Democrats
item.description:
Bobby Pulido, a moderate Democrat and Latin Grammy Award-winning Tejano musician, ousted Representative Monica De La Cruz, a three-term Texas Republican, early Wednesday, according to The Associated Press, signaling a deep backlash to Republicans and President Trump among Latino voters.

The South Texas border district that Mr. Pulido won was seen as a bellwether for Latino voter sentiment. Mr. Trump won it by 18 percentage points in 2024, as residents lashed out against inflation and the Biden administration’s immigration policies.

Mr. Pulido said in an interview during the campaign that when he began his bid, “nobody thought I had a chance” because the district had so heavily favored Mr. Trump.

But this year, Mr. Trump’s immigration crackdown and the high cost of gas and groceries, as well as deep cuts to Medicaid in a district reliant on the program, spurred voter anger.

Mr. Pulido became the subject of international media attention as he performed for free at quinceañeras and other local parties as part of his outreach to low-propensity voters.

He also cut a distinctive profile, pitching himself as a conservative “Blue Dog” Democrat who supported a secure border, owned guns and loved God while also promoting Democratic visions for government-funded health care and safety net programs.

Ms. De La Cruz attacked Mr. Pulido over offensive statements he had made in the past, including about postpartum women’s bodies, and his connection to a former bandmate who is a sex offender. But in the end, she could not overcome Mr. Trump’s unpopularity and Mr. Pulido’s popularity.
