item.title: Moderate Republican Loses Seat in Pennsylvania Swing District
item.description:
Representative Brian Fitzpatrick of Pennsylvania, one of the House’s most moderate Republicans, lost his bid for re-election early Wednesday, according to The Associated Press. He had spent a decade as one of his party’s strongest survivors in a Democratic-leaning district.

Bob Harvie, a Bucks County commissioner, mobilized voters in the district outside of Philadelphia with a message that it was time to boot Mr. Fitzpatrick, and ensure a Democratic majority in Congress to check Mr. Trump’s power.

Mr. Harvie campaigned with Representative Hakeem Jeffries of New York, the House Democratic leader, and the state’s governor, Josh Shapiro, among others. Before the election, Mr. Harvie told voters that he hoped to ride “those Josh Shapiro coattails” to the House.

Mr. Fitzpatrick, a five-term incumbent, had been the only congressional Republican to win re-election three times — 2016, 2020 and 2024 — in a district that did not vote for President Trump, and he broke with Mr. Trump more often than most Republicans.

At one point, the president complained about Mr. Fitzpatrick’s then-fiancée, a White House correspondent for Fox News, citing her soon-to-be husband’s voting record.

“Her husband votes against me all the time. Can you imagine?” Mr. Trump said, adding, “He likes voting against Trump. You know what happens with that. It doesn’t work out well.”

The outcome is a big win for Democrats, who couldn’t defeat Mr. Fitzpatrick in 2018 even as they swept to power in a blue wave. His defeat means that Mr. Harvie is likely to hold the seat for years as the Philadelphia suburbs become more Democratic.

Democrats poured in money late in the race and worked aggressively to tie Mr. Fitzpatrick to Mr. Trump. Mr. Fitzpatrick had campaigned as a different kind of Republican, and he had the support of many groups that typically support Democrats, including labor unions and environmental organizations.

The seat had been in the Fitzpatrick family for most of the last two decades.

Mr. Fitzpatrick, a former F.B.I. agent, had succeeded his brother, Mike Fitzpatrick, who died in 2020.

item.title: Collins Falls to Jackson in Maine, Ending a Three-Decade Senate Tenure
item.description:
Senator Susan Collins, Republican of Maine, lost her seat of three decades on Wednesday to Troy Jackson, a Democratic former state legislator, according to a New York Times projection. The defeat ended the run of the sole sitting Republican member of Congress from New England.

Ms. Collins rose to the upper echelons of the Senate as she defied the leftward tilt of her state, but ultimately could not overcome voters’ strong resistance to President Trump in what became one of the nation’s costliest, hardest-fought and most closely watched Senate races.

The victory adds to a new Democratic majority in the Senate and vindicated the party’s long-held hopes of ousting Ms. Collins, despite a tumultuous race in which intraparty divisions had threatened to dash their chances.

Democratic leaders’ initial chosen candidate, the moderate Gov. Janet Mills, failed to gain traction and suspended her campaign, and months later the party primary winner, Graham Platner, dropped out after allegations of sexual assault surfaced.

Mr. Jackson entered the race in July, when he was chosen after Mr. Platner’s exit.

The defeat of Ms. Collins, the chairwoman of the powerful Senate Appropriations Committee, will lessen Maine’s influence in Congress given her seniority and longtime role as a more moderate Republican linchpin on much of the significant legislation in the Senate. She has directed tens of billions of dollars in federal funding to her state for everything from fire stations to shipbuilding.

But opposition to the Trump administration ran deep in Maine, where the president’s tariffs on Canada had a major impact and disrupted an economy that relies on a significant amount of commerce crossing the border.

“It has been the honor of my life to serve the people of Maine in the United States Senate,” she said in a concession statement. “I’m proud of all I have been able to accomplish for our state and for our country in the past 30 years.”

Ms. Collins battled the perception that she too often yielded to Mr. Trump, even though she was the member of her party who broke with him most often in the Senate. Some Maine voters who had repeatedly supported Ms. Collins said they would not do so this year, hoping to create a more formidable obstacle to the president and his policies.

Ms. Collins was the only Republican senator running for re-election this year in a state Mr. Trump lost to Kamala Harris in 2024.

Mr. Jackson, who lost Maine’s Democratic primary for governor before becoming the Senate nominee, questioned the influence of Ms. Collins, portrayed her as an enabler of Mr. Trump and promised to be an impediment to the Trump administration. Both were from largely rural Aroostook County in the less populated northern reaches of the state.

Ms. Collins, 73, was a former Senate aide and a Small Business Administration official under President George H.W. Bush. After losing a race for Maine governor in 1994, she won the Senate seat in 1996 and has held it since despite furious Democratic efforts to unseat her. She has not missed a roll-call vote in her tenure, a formidable achievement, and this year cast her 10,000th vote.

In the Senate, she has been an essential part of a shrinking group of more centrist Republicans who were willing to occasionally break with their party and, in recent years, with Mr. Trump on health and economic policy as well as a handful of nominees.

She was a critical vote to prevent Senate repeal of the Affordable Care Act in 2017 and opposed the nomination of Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. Her breaks with the White House have angered the president, who often lashed out at her.

But to Democrats and Mr. Jackson, it was not enough. They accused her of bowing to the president and opposing him only when her vote would not seal the outcome. Ms. Collins, who supports abortion rights, came under particularly heavy fire from Mr. Jackson and Democratic activists for her vote in 2018 to confirm Justice Brett M. Kavanaugh, who later joined a Supreme Court majority in overturning Roe v. Wade.

item.description:
“America is back,” declared Representative Hakeem Jeffries, Democrat of New York and the minority leader, on Tuesday night as Democrats were on the path to a resounding victory in the House. “Today begins the great American comeback.”

Mr. Jeffries, a reserved politician who grew up in a working-class home in the Crown Heights section of Brooklyn in the 1980s, ended on a note of hometown pride.

item.title: How Ken Paxton Went From Republican Survivor to Republican Liability
item.description:
Ken Paxton had survived indictment, impeachment and years of scandal. He counted on surviving another election.

For more than a decade, the Republican attorney general of Texas won election after election despite rarely campaigning, dismissing accusations of adultery, bribery and fraud as partisan attacks.

But his bid for U.S. Senate ended in defeat against his foil, James Talarico, a Democrat who tied Mr. Paxton’s scandals to the rising costs facing Texans.

Mr. Talarico, 37, drew support from voters in both parties with an energetic campaign that relentlessly tried to make Mr. Paxton’s scandals feel tangible to voters. His victory marked the first Senate win for a Texas Democrat since 1988 — the year before Mr. Talarico was born.

In a short concession speech at his watch party in Dallas on Tuesday night, Mr. Paxton said he was grateful for the 12 years he spent as attorney general and wished Mr. Talarico well.

“The best part of it is the memories of working with so many great Texans,” Mr. Paxton said. “As soon as I’m out of office, I still have a lot of friends in Texas.”

Mr. Paxton’s loss underscored a midterm election season where many voters who had soured on the economic and foreign policy choices of President Trump put their pocketbooks over their party.

Mr. Paxton, 63, leaves behind a checkered, but lasting, legacy. He sued the Obama and Biden administrations more than 100 times, influencing state and federal policy on issues such as abortion, immigration and L.G.B.T.Q. rights. He also challenged the 2020 presidential election results, securing him the loyalty of Mr. Trump.

Mr. Paxton also helped purge Texas of Republican moderates and push his party further to the right, with the help of a few far right megadonors.

But Mr. Paxton’s career was shadowed by scandal — an indictment, an impeachment and allegations of two extramarital relationships — that cost him key allies and donors who grew tired of defending him. Elon Musk and national Republican groups spent tens of millions of dollars on ads to try to shore him up, but to no avail.

To be sure, the outcome of the Senate race was as much about Mr. Talarico’s assets as it was about Mr. Paxton’s liabilities. But in a state that was supposed to be reliably Republican, the fingers in the state’s G.O.P. have already begun pointing to the biggest loser.

As a standard-bearer for his party’s far right contingent in Texas, Mr. Paxton had become known as “Teflon Ken,” the man who, despite his many problems, always pulled out a win. Now, he is the face of the worst Republican wipeout in mdoern Texas history.

“People will study this campaign failure, this ridiculous candidate, for decades,” said Matt Mackowiak, a Republican strategist who worked on the campaign of incumbent Senator John Cornyn, whom Mr. Paxton defeated in the Republican primary in May. “Every single person that had a chance to stop this when it could have been stopped is to blame.”

Mr. Paxton was far from the only Republican to lose in Texas. From governor to state judges, Republicans fell short up and down the ballot in Texas and across the country.

“It’s a bloodbath, everywhere,” Matt Wolking, an adviser to a super PAC backing Mr. Paxton, said at his watch party.

Mr. Paxton had risen by challenging his party’s establishment, aligning himself with far-right activists in the Texas House and winning the attorney general’s office in 2014 with support from Senator Ted Cruz and the Tea Party.

When Mr. Paxton was indicted on charges of defrauding investors in a technology firm in 2015, he smiled in his mug shot. To his critics, the image captured his apparent indifference to the allegations.

The fraud case hung over him for years, but opponents failed to make it disqualifying. He won re-election in 2018 and again in 2022.

Backed by billionaire donors Tim Dunn and Farris Wilks, Mr. Paxton emphasized his fights against Democrats and his alliance with Mr. Trump, often ignoring his opponents and refusing debates.

“The reports of my demise have been greatly exaggerated,” Mr. Paxton joked during his victory speech in 2022.

Mr. Paxton faced the most serious threat to his career in 2020, from within his innermost circle.

That October, senior aides reported him to the F.B.I., accusing him of doing favors for a campaign donor in exchange for home renovations and a job for a woman with whom he was allegedly having an affair.

Mr. Paxton denied wrongdoing and fired four of the aides, who sued his agency under the state’s whistle-blower law. The agency agreed to a $3.3 million settlement, subject to legislative approval.

Chip Roy, a Republican congressman who once worked under Mr. Paxton in the attorney general’s office, said Mr. Paxton’s “leadership problems” drove away senior employees at the agency.

“When you treat the office of AG as a personal and political playground, people inside and out tend to notice,” he told The New York Times after Mr. Paxton’s loss.

Faced with these new corruption allegations, Mr. Paxton drew closer to Mr. Trump. In December 2020, he asked the U.S. Supreme Court to throw out the presidential election results in four states won by Joseph R. Biden Jr., seeking to overturn Mr. Trump’s defeat.

Mr. Paxton lost that fight, but gained Mr. Trump’s loyalty. He spent the next four years suing to block the Biden administration’s policies on immigration, abortion and other issues.

But his request for state funding to settle the whistle-blower lawsuit rekindled problems in his home state and prompted a Texas House investigation. In May 2023, a majority of House Republicans joined Democrats to impeach him on corruption charges.

After a 10-day trial in the Texas Senate, Mr. Paxton was acquitted, largely along party lines. His wife, now a state senator, was recused from voting.

The next spring, Mr. Paxton settled the 2015 securities fraud case against him. He never faced a jury and did not admit guilt.

“I learned early on how utterly corrupt and amoral Ken Paxton is. And tonight he finally had to answer for it,” Brian Wice, a Houston attorney who prosecuted the securities fraud case against Mr. Paxton, said Tuesday night.

Survival actually buoyed Mr. Paxton’s power in Texas, and his hubris.

He began to travel more, spending tens of thousands of dollars on trips to South Africa, India and Taiwan. He began dating a second woman, a Christian influencer and registered Democrat from Louisiana. He helped oust some of the Republicans who had voted to impeach him.

In 2024, Mr. Trump was elected to a second term, and Mr. Paxton turned his sights to a higher prize: the U.S. Senate.

Mr. Trump remained an X factor. For weeks ahead of the Republican primary runoff, Mr. Trump withheld his endorsement. He eventually backed Mr. Paxton, citing his loyalty, and Mr. Paxton bested Mr. Cornyn by more than 30 points. At his watch party, Mr. Paxton thanked Mr. Trump.

“When everyone in Washington told him to abandon me,” Mr. Paxton said, “he didn’t listen.”

But Mr. Paxton’s fortunes faltered with the president’s. Mr. Talarico, a Christian seminarian and former teacher, ran on an expansive and detailed economic platform that centered the cost of food, housing and health care. He also made the corruption allegations newly relevant.

“He now owns 15 homes, while most Texans can’t afford one,” Mr. Talarico said on the campaign trail, referencing Mr. Paxton’s growing real estate portfolio.

As polls began favoring Mr. Talarico, Mr. Paxton shifted his message, emphasizing his modest upbringing in a military family. He launched a statewide tour, appearing with Mr. Trump and Mr. Cruz. Mr. Musk eventually came to his aid, funneling hundreds of millions of dollars into ads.

As Election Day neared, Mr. Paxton returned to his partisan attacks, warning conservative voters a win for Mr. Talarico would mean the end of conservative, Christian values in the state of Texas.

But the momentum failed to materialize.

In the final weeks of the race, Mr. Paxton invoked the imagery of the Texas Revolution to rally his supporters. Lt. Gov. Dan Patrick compared the Republican ticket to the defenders of the Alamo.

Those men lost their battle nearly 190 years ago, just as Mr. Paxton did on Tuesday. Whether this was his last stand remained an open question.

In his concession speech on Tuesday, Mr. Paxton said, “We’ve had a difficult night across the country but it’s not over.”

item.title: Across the Country, Voters Give Direct Orders to State Governments
item.description:
As voters chose state and local officials on Tuesday, many also weighed in on how future elections would be run and how their own votes would be counted.

In a show of disgust over the role of “dark money” in politics, Montana voters approved a ballot measure to ban corporations, nonprofits and labor unions from doing business in the state if they had made political contributions. The result appears likely to create a legal test of Citizens United, the Supreme Court decision that said independent political spending by businesses is protected free speech.

Michigan voters approved a similar measure, deciding to bar electric and gas utilities as well as many government contractors from making political donations.

In Virginia, voters backed a constitutional amendment to restore voting rights to people convicted of felonies upon their release. In Utah, they rejected a measure that would have raised the share of votes needed to approve certain changes to taxes.

Voters protected their right to propose ballot initiatives with a constitutional amendment in Montana, and raised the bar for state lawmakers to alter voter-backed initiatives in Missouri. And in South Dakota, they rebuffed an effort to require a 60 percent supermajority vote to amend their state’s constitution.

In Massachusetts, voters rejected a proposition that would have ended closed-party primaries and instead allowed all candidates to appear on the same ballot, with the top two vote-getters advancing.

Measures to ban noncitizen voting or require voters to present identification also passed in a few states — West Virginia, Arkansas, South Dakota and Ohio — with more votes still being counted into the early morning Wednesday. But voter identification initiatives were rejected in Colorado and California.

In Maryland, voters cleared a path for a new congressional map that could boost Democratic representation in 2028. In Missouri, they rejected a redrawn map that could have provided Republicans an advantage. Those moves followed a redistricting blitz that came at the urging of President Trump, with the intention of gaining more Republican seats. Ultimately, the efforts did not stave off significant Democratic victories.

“Given the blue wave it’s basically what you’d expect — voters blocking a Republican gerrymander in Missouri and greenlighting a future Democratic gerrymander in Maryland,” Nicholas Stephanopoulos, a Harvard Law School professor, said in a text message. “It’s a partisan story, not one of consistency with respect to redistricting.”

The election measures were a sizable chunk of the more than 140 statewide ballot questions that gave voters the opportunity to set policy directly on Tuesday, on issues ranging from abortion and transgender rights to taxation and affordability.

Many of the measures were handed down by state lawmakers for voter approval. Others were written by voters themselves, often with a goal of changing or creating policies that their representatives otherwise wouldn’t have taken up.

As the focus shifts to the 2028 presidential election, how the initiatives performed will help set the tone for political debate by pointing to the issues that were important to midterm voters.

In Missouri, voters rejected an attempt by state lawmakers to repeal a constitutional right to abortion, recently approved by voters, by pairing the initiative with a ban on gender-transition care for minors.

Virginia voters enshrined abortion rights into their state’s constitution and repealed a ban on same-sex marriage, safeguarding the right should the Supreme Court overturn it in the future.

In Nebraska, voters passed restrictions on transgender students’ participation in sports. Voters’ views on transgender rights were also tested in deep-blue states on Tuesday with initiatives in Washington State and Colorado.

In Alabama, voters passed a measure requiring public schools to have pupils recite the Pledge of Allegiance every day and allow for student-led prayer. They also approved an initiative requiring public schools to play or arrange for a performance of the first stanza of “The Star-Spangled Banner” once every week.

A Florida ballot measure to cut homeowners’ property taxes also passed. Opponents said that limiting property taxes would tighten a major source of funding for services like police and fire departments and programs for low-income residents. But supporters billed it as a way to provide relief for homeowners as the cost of living has ballooned.

item.title: Americans on Why They Rejected Trump’s Republican Party
item.description:
From Texas to Maine, Democratic voters thronged to the polls on Tuesday. Independents turned their backs on President Trump. And Republicans seemed to be slipping out of the thrall of a president who has defined American politics for a decade.

In interviews and at the ballot box, voters declared that they were unhappy with the way things were going in their country and wanted a change.

In 2024, Joshua Buchanan, 39, a train-design engineer in Woodruff, S.C., voted for Mr. Trump. Two years later, he had regrets.

“I probably made the wrong choice,” said Mr. Buchanan, who this time voted for Annie Andrews, the Democratic candidate for Senate. Her victory over the Trump-endorsed Republican, Darline Graham, would have been unimaginable not that long ago.

Donald Trump took the American political system by storm a decade ago, electrifying working-class voters with his hard-edge populist message. But as the back half of his second term draws near, his job approval has collapsed under the weight of unpopular economic policies and a war with Iran.

Democrats, who were dejected just two years ago, vibrated with fury — and determination to go to the polls. The actual candidates for governor, Senate or the House could seem almost secondary.

“I would crawl on my belly over broken glass to vote against that awful man,” said Ronan Donohoe, 85, a retired high school history teacher in Portsmouth, N.H.

He said his vote on Tuesday for Democrats was about “letting everybody know that we are fed up with everything the Trump administration stands for, and that we want better.”

In interviews, voters often expressed frustration with how much life costs. Prices are still considerably higher than before the pandemic, but voters said that Mr. Trump, who had promised to lower prices in 2024, now seemed to shrug off their concerns.

“He wouldn’t know what it is to pull into a gas station and put gas in your car,” said Suzanne Murray, 78, a retired hairdresser in Phoenix. “He wouldn’t know what it is to go into a grocery store and buy groceries on a limited income.”

She added: “He’s so reckless with the United States.”

Ms. Murray has leaned toward Democrats, but Republicans expressed exasperation with Mr. Trump, too. The reasons included affordability, the Epstein files and corruption. And a number of more traditional Republicans said in interviews that they no longer recognized their party.

“The Republican Party has lost its way,” said Van Z. Hampton, 71, a registered Republican in Dodge City, Kansas, who said he had voted straight ticket Democrat the first time since Jimmy Carter in 1976. Mr. Hampton, a retired Kansas state judge, voted for Mr. Trump twice, but has become repelled by what he described as unbridled corruption.

“The ship was hijacked by thieves,” he said referring to the Trump administration’s stewardship of the U.S. government. “It’s going in the wrong direction — toward their shore to loot it and unload it.”

For Dan Bailey, a sanitation driver from Glen Cove, N.Y, it was Mr. Trump’s casual brushoff of the Epstein files, and Mr. Trump’s cabinet, who included, he said, “a secretary of war who doesn’t know anything about war.”

“I am so fed up with being lied to,” said Mr. Bailey, who said he hasn’t voted for much of his adult life, but showed up and voted straight ticket Democrat on Tuesday. “I feel that there has to be some sort of change. I’m hoping my little bit can make a difference.”

While the night may have delivered a sweeping win for Democrats, it was far from a mandate. Many Republicans and independents said they defected simply to stop a president they say no longer represents them.

Mr. Hampton, the retired Kansas judge, for example, had advice for Democrats who won on Tuesday: They won votes “not because we love you, but because we need you to do the right thing. Be wise about support you got.”

Many voters expressed deep discomfort about where they fit in the political system. Many said they felt politically homeless. Mr. Trump has so defined the Republican Party that it was hard to predict what it would mean when he leaves office. And many voters also struggled to define the Democratic Party, beyond its opposition to Mr. Trump.

“There’s no Republicans or Democrats anymore,” said A.J. Asci, 49, who works in the hotel industry in Savannah, Ga. “America looks more confusing than ever.”

Mr. Asci immigrated from Turkey and became a citizen 18 years ago. He said he had learned everything about life in America from his neighbor at the time, whom he still visits in a nursing home. But life in America today feels unstable: He does not think he will be able to afford to retire here.

And he thinks the money flooding into politics is gumming up the wheels of American democracy.

“You cannot get justice and uphold the laws if you get paid by somebody else,” he said. “It’s a crooked system.”

Many voters talked about their distress at the vitriol that has overtaken political discourse, and said they voted in part to counter it.

Sheldon McCormick, 68, a handyman standing outside his polling station in Waldo, Maine, said he would vote for anybody who stood up for civility.

“For me, decency can go a long way,” he said. “There’s good in the world, and it’s time to get back to it.”

A registered independent, Mr. McCormick said he split his ticket, voting for Susan Collins, the Republican senator, and Matt Dunlap, the Democratic candidate for Congress.

Lamont Fisher, 46, an independent voter in Austin, Texas, expressed similar distaste for the country’s angry politics.

“Why be so extreme that we can’t accept someone else’s viewpoints?” said Mr. Fisher, a broadband network tech who grew up in a Republican family. “We’re all in the same country at the end of the day.”

He said he had voted for James Talarico, who will be the first Democratic senator from Texas in decades.

“His view is, I want purple,” Mr. Fisher said. “That’s what I believe in too.”

Not everyone feels that way. A number of G.O.P. voters said they were perfectly happy with Mr. Trump, and voted the straight Republican ticket with a light heart.

“I don’t live with the guy,” said Ofelia Armendarez, a registrar clerk at an elementary school in Visalia, Calif., who voted for Trump three times. “If he’s doing the job correctly, that’s all that matters to me.”

One of their biggest concerns was a takeover by democratic socialists, which far eclipsed any frustration with Mr. Trump.

Patricia Fay, 69, a retired software engineer in Phoenix, said she does not typically vote a straight Republican ticket, but did on Tuesday.

“I don’t want Arizona to become another New York or Southern California,” she said. Socialists, she said, want “everything for free.”

Still, others were excited about progressive candidates.

Jeff Fawaz, 42, who owns oil change and auto shops in Dearborn, Mich., voted for Mr. Trump twice, because of his promises to stop wars and help small business owners. “I just believed him,” he said of Mr. Trump. Now, he thinks that “he’s the most bought and paid-for president I’ve ever seen.”

On Tuesday, he voted for the Democrat for Senate, Dr. Abdul El-Sayed.

Jillian Anthony, Murray Carpenter, Jonathan J. Higuera, Ryan Patrick Hooper, Caitlin Philippo, Nate Schweber, Sabrina Shankman and Tiffany Tan contributed reporting.

item.title: How Gina Hinojosa Captured Texas
item.description:
Gina Hinojosa seemed to come out of nowhere when she announced her run for Texas governor a year ago.

As a Democratic state lawmaker from Austin, she supported transgender rights and opposed enshrining the state’s income tax ban in the Texas Constitution — causes that kept her little known and far from the state’s centers of power.

The well-funded campaign of incumbent Greg Abbott, one of America’s most powerful Republicans, refused to say her name even as her campaign gained momentum over the summer, allowing her to define herself to voters on her own terms.

On Tuesday, Ms. Hinojosa denied Mr. Abbott a record-setting fourth term. She became the first Democrat to win statewide office in more than 30 years and the first Latina to be elected governor in Texas.

“Latinas led the charge,” said Maria Teresa Kumar, president of Voto Latino, a voter advocacy group. “We saw Latino participation in Texas surpass 2024 number. You don’t see that happen.”

“The candidates were speaking to the Latino experience. People who voted for Trump said, ‘This is not what I voted for,’” said Ms. Kumar, referring to the cost of living and President Trump’s aggressive immigration crackdown.

Ms. Hinojosa, 52, a native of the Rio Grande Valley, foresaw what others missed: The state’s Latino plurality — and a rural population that had been seen as a Republican redoubt — were ready for someone like her in the governor’s mansion.

Ms. Hinojosa is a civil rights and labor lawyer who spent nearly a decade in the statehouse, representing a solidly Democratic district and championing long-shot issues. In this year’s campaign, she embraced a more populist message and Mr. Abbott failed to make her more progressive policies into political millstones.

In the end, like many competitive elections this year, the race for governor of Texas became a referendum on affordability. Ms. Hinojosa successfully argued that Republicans, who have controlled every branch of state government for more than two decades, were not prioritizing the cost of living.

Ian Hogan, a 38-year-old Austin construction manager, said he had voted for Ms. Hinojosa primarily on economic grounds.

“Trump has caused some pretty serious issues with inflation and war and gas prices,” he said Tuesday, adding, “How expensive are things going to get?”

The last woman to occupy the governor’s mansion was Ann Richards, who left office in 1995. Anabel Lopez, 61, of San Antonio, said that she had longed to see a Latina become governor.

“I dreamed for a long time for a moment like this,” Ms. Lopez said. “This is monumental for Texas. We want change. We needed to send new people to represent us in the government. The Republicans had become too extreme.”

Latinos, who make up the largest ethnic population in the state, were a crucial part of Ms. Hinojosa’s coalition. Many soured on President Trump after voting for him in unprecedented numbers in 2024.

Their numbers have only grown in importance in the past two decades. In 2024, there were 6.3 million eligible Latino voters in Texas, up from three million in 2000, according to the UCLA Latino Policy and Politics Institute.

Some of Mr. Trump’s greatest gains in 2024 were along the Texas border, where he flipped several majority-Hispanic counties. But Ms. Hinojosa greatly outperformed Kamala Harris’ margins in the region: Cameron County, along the Mexican border, shifted 40 percentage points to the left.

Latina candidates have been making inroads throughout Texas in the past several election cycles. In 2018, Democrats Veronica Escobar, and Sylvia Garcia became the first Latinas elected from Texas to the U.S. House of Representatives, both from districts where Latinos are the majority of the population.

In 2022, Monica De La Cruz, a Republican, won a once-Democratic border district, though she lost Tuesday to a moderate Democrat, Tejano singer Bobby Pulido.

Ms. Hinojosa’s win followed years of tantalizing near-misses for Democrats seeking the governor’s office. In 2010, a few summer polls suggested a competitive race between Bill White, a Democrat, and Gov. Rick Perry, a Republican. By the fall, Mr. Perry was consistently leading in the polls, and he won by nearly 13 points.

In 2022, several polls had Beto O’Rourke just five points behind Mr. Abbott. But Mr. Abbott’s polling lead grew that fall, and Mr. O’Rourke lost by nearly 11 points.

Ms. Hinojosa has said that she never intended to run for political office, much less for governor.

She first ran for office in 2011, seeking a seat on the school board after state budget cuts threatened to close an elementary school that one of her sons attended. She later became a state legislator representing one of the most liberal districts in the state.

As a governor candidate, Ms. Hinojosa made public schools and concerns over affordability and her opposition to data centers centerpieces of her campaign. Those issues resonated with Latino and former republican voters alike.

Armando Gomez, an immigrant from Mexico who has lived in Texas for 25 years, said he had come out to vote for Democrats on Tuesday for “a better economy.”

Mr. Gomez, 66, who works as a contractor in Austin, believes the country has devolved during President Trump’s second term, and said the war in Iran is driving up prices. “Everything is too expensive,” he said, citing his rising health insurance premium and electricity and mortgage bills.

He particularly relished voting against Mr. Abbott and Ken Paxton, whose Senate campaign ended in a drubbing.

“I don’t like Abbott and Paxton,” he added. “Two hypocrites.”

Madaleine Rubin, David Montgomery and Jillian Anthony contributed reporting.

item.title: Democrats Seize Control of Congress, Ending a G.O.P. Trifecta
item.description:
Democrats won control of the House early Wednesday, capping a sweeping takeover of Congress as they harnessed a backlash against President Trump to end Republicans’ governing trifecta and secure a powerful foothold from which to check his power.

Capitalizing on widespread dissatisfaction over the war in Iran, Mr. Trump’s tariffs and corruption allegations, Democrats won decisive victories across the country, reaching deep into Republican territory where voters had soured on the president and his allies.

Having won control of the Senate despite a map stacked against them, Democrats early Wednesday clinched the 218 seats needed to take control of the House of Representatives, according to The Associated Press, and appeared on track to capture many more.

With final results still outstanding, it was unclear exactly how large Democrats’ majority would be, a factor that will shape their ability to set an agenda and muscle bills through the Senate, where Republicans retained the ability to block major measures from the minority.

But in a thrashing for the G.O.P., Democrats had won decisive victories across the country, including in solid conservative bastions, in what was projected early Wednesday morning to be the largest popular vote victory for either party since 1976.

The election results promised a new era of divided government in Washington and a freshly assertive Congress after two years in which Republicans generally ceded power to Mr. Trump and reduced the legislative branch’s role to that of a mere bystander. It capped a fiercely fought midterm election cycle that Democrats entered chastened from the 2024 presidential election but finished buoyant and with strong political winds at their backs.

“The American people have spoken and made clear they’ve had enough of the extremism, enough of the corruption,” Representative Hakeem Jeffries, the Democratic minority leader who is now in line to be speaker, told supporters in Washington. “They want a Congress that’s going to deliver for the American people.”

Senator Chuck Schumer, the New York Democrat and the longtime leader who was deeply involved in his party’s uphill battle for the majority, vowed a swift change in direction.

“We have five words for the American people,” he told reporters in Washington. “Relief is on the way.”

With control of Congress and its committees, Democrats are expected to deploy their oversight powers to aggressively investigate Mr. Trump and his administration over allegations of corruption, aggressive immigration enforcement tactics and the president’s pardons.

Representative Robert Garcia, the California Democrat who is poised to be the chairman of the Oversight Committee, the main investigative panel in the House, issued a warning in a statement on Tuesday night.

“Lawyer up,” he said.

Democrats have also promised a shock-and-awe legislative sprint in which they plan to push through bills that would restore health care subsidies and Medicaid funding, address the increased costs of food and fuel and seek to force Mr. Trump to roll back his tariffs and end the war with Iran.

Democratic control of the Senate will also give the party veto power over Mr. Trump’s judicial and administration nominees, as well as the leadership of the committees that will have the authority to subpoena administration officials and others.

Mr. Trump, who appeared stunned by the results even as he deflected any blame for the losses, insisted he would still have the upper hand over a Democratic Congress.

“I have total veto power, so they have to come to us,” he said in an interview with The New York Times as the Democratic victories piled up. “And if they have some good ideas, I’m certainly open to working.”

Despite their losses in the last presidential election, Democrats had been consistently bullish about their ability to win the House majority. The party out of power typically gains seats in midterm elections, and Republicans have held only a slender majority in the House since they took over in 2023.

They were less optimistic about their prospects in the Senate, where the political map was stacked against them with seats in states that had become solidly Republican during the Trump era.

But as voters who backed Mr. Trump in 2024 began souring on the president and his agenda, Democrats saw an opportunity to drastically expand their political map. They won in longtime G.O.P. bastions like Kansas and Texas, reversed years of losses in Iowa and Ohio, and flipped both North Carolina and South Carolina.

Mr. Schumer recalled that when he first began talking about reclaiming the majority in 2025, “people rolled their eyes.” Democrats, he argued, prevailed because they heeded voters who were frustrated with how things were going in Washington and felt ignored by Republicans.

“We listened; they didn’t,” he said. “And the American people reduced the red brick wall to a pile of bricks.”

Their victories were powered by Americans’ growing dismay over the rising costs of goods and fuel linked to Mr. Trump’s tariffs and the war. Democrats painted the G.O.P. as beholden to the president and indifferent to the financial struggles of everyday Americans.

Those arguments were bolstered by growing concerns among voters about corruption in Washington and the cuts to Medicaid and health care subsidies that Republicans enacted as part of their signature tax cut and domestic policy package last year.

Their strength became evident early in the night, when Democrats surged in crucial House battlegrounds and had notched victories in competitive races in Florida, Pennsylvania and North Carolina. The party needed a net gain of only three seats to win the House.

Aware of the historical trend, Republicans had taken efforts to stem their expected losses with a frenzy of redistricting in red states that was meant to increase the number of G.O.P.-leaning districts and force Democrats out of what had been safe seats.

But those moves fell short in the face of Mr. Trump’s plummeting approval ratings. In Florida, Democrats won in three districts that Republican state lawmakers redrew to favor their party, including some where Mr. Trump won by more than 10 percentage points in 2024.

Even with many races uncalled, Speaker Mike Johnson effectively acknowledged his party’s defeat on Tuesday night.

“We knew that to keep the House and sustain our majority, we would have to defy more than a century of midterm history,” Mr. Johnson said. “It’s very, very difficult to overcome. And it looks like history will be kept tonight.”

The drubbing appeared to leave many Republicans reeling on Tuesday evening, and raised questions about the direction that the party would take in the final two years of Mr. Trump’s second term, a lame-duck period that has bedeviled many presidents.

Senator John Thune of South Dakota, the Republican leader, said his party would work to thwart Democrats at every turn.

“As we head into 2027, Senate Republicans will not stand idly by as the far-left, socialist wing of the Democrat party attempts to unwind everything we’ve done,” Mr. Thune said in a statement early Wednesday. “Thankfully, we still have President Trump in the White House, and we’ll work with him to stop the worst impulses of Democrat extremism. We cannot let their fringe positions become the mainstream.”

During the first half of his second term, Mr. Trump has enjoyed near-total control of Congress, with lawmakers showing little appetite for imposing guardrails on his actions.

But Senate races in particular suggested that Mr. Trump had lost his once dominant sway over Republican voters. The president won both North Carolina and South Carolina in all three of his presidential elections. But in both cases in this election, his handpicked candidates trailed significantly.

And with Mr. Trump losing ground even in Ohio and Iowa, two former battleground states that he transformed into G.O.P. strongholds, it was unclear whether he would exhibit the same hold on Republican lawmakers that has characterized his second term.

Sensing a political shift in the final weeks of their campaigns, many vulnerable lawmakers sought to put some distance between themselves and his policies, particularly his signature tariffs. But the pivot appeared to have come too late.

Annie Karni and Robert Jimison contributed reporting from Washington.

item.title: Jocelyn Benson Holds Michigan Governor’s Office for Democrats
item.description:
Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson won the race for governor in Michigan on Wednesday, according to The Associated Press, keeping in Democratic hands an office that has an important role in certifying the closely divided state’s presidential election results.

Ms. Benson, 49, will take over in January from Gov. Gretchen Whitmer, a Democrat who was barred by term limits from running again, and who built a national profile during eight years in Lansing. Ms. Benson defeated Representative John James, a Republican from suburban Detroit who had lost two previous statewide campaigns.

Both candidates made an anti-incumbent case to an electorate frustrated by the high cost of living and rising prices.

While Mr. James blamed the Democrats in state government, Ms. Benson criticized President Trump’s policies, including tariffs targeting Canada that have had an outsized effect on Michigan’s auto industry. She pledged to seek “sub-national” agreements with Canada, which borders Michigan, if elected.

“At a time where it feels like, at the federal level, government is showing up everywhere we don’t want it and nowhere where we actually need it, I will make sure that government is showing up for you and doing right by you,” Ms. Benson said in a recent debate hosted by WDIV-TV.

Ms. Benson, a former law school dean who served two terms as Michigan’s chief elections officer, became a target of right-wing activists in 2020 when she presided over Joseph R. Biden Jr.’s victory in the state over Mr. Trump. Ms. Benson defended the results against unproven claims of widespread fraud. After Mr. Trump returned to office, she fought his administration’s efforts to obtain private voter data.

Michigan’s governor signs a document certifying the state’s presidential electors, a role that could again become important if the results of a future presidential race are contested. Mr. Trump carried the state in 2016 and 2024, while Mr. Biden won it in 2020.

Ms. Benson will become the first Democratic governor of Michigan to succeed a fellow Democrat since the 1960s. She will also be the third woman to serve as the state’s leader.

The governor’s race had initially been expected to be a three-way contest including Mike Duggan, a former mayor of Detroit and longtime Democrat who was running as an independent. Though he received significant endorsements and had competitive polling numbers, Mr. Duggan dropped out of the race in May, saying he did not want to be a spoiler. His decision to withdraw was widely seen as a boost for Democrats.

item.title: Max Miller Loses in Ohio After Ex-Wife’s Abuse Allegations
item.description:
Representative Max Miller, the Ohio Republican whose campaign was rocked by accusations that he physically abused his ex-wife and young daughter, lost his re-election bid, according to The Associated Press, handing Democrats a seat in deep-red territory as they won House control.

Brian Poindexter, a union ironworker, defeated Mr. Miller, a two-term congressman whose political rise was fueled by his close relationship with President Trump, in a district Mr. Trump won by a double-digit margin two years ago. Mr. Miller had rejected calls by fellow Republicans to drop out of the race after he was accused by his ex-wife, Emily Moreno, of domestic abuse against her and their 2-year-old daughter.

Ms. Moreno, the daughter of Senator Bernie Moreno, also an Ohio Republican, said that Mr. Miller had scalded her chest and stomach by throwing hot water from a skillet at her body; held a gun to her head; pushed her against a wall and hit her head; and fractured their daughter’s collarbone and bruised her shoulder. The allegations came to light as part of a lengthy divorce court battle.

Mr. Miller denied all of the accusations and embarked on a defiant media tour in which he accused his ex-wife of being mentally unstable, a liar, a stalker and a dangerous individual.

As the sordid family drama gained national attention, some powerful Ohio Republicans, including Senator Jon Husted, pressed Mr. Miller to exit the race and resign. Mr. Moreno, who at first tried to avoid questions about Mr. Miller, eventually said that his former son-in-law was not fit to hold public office.

“If there are any basic standards of character required to hold elected office, Max Miller fails them,” Mr. Moreno said in an emotional statement. The House Ethics Committee also opened a review of the domestic abuse allegations.

Some White House officials wanted Mr. Miller to drop out of the race in time for Republicans to replace him on the ballot, but the president stopped short of asking Mr. Miller to drop out.

In a private phone call, Mr. Trump simply warned him that it might be difficult for him to win given the allegations. Mr. Miller was resolute that he would do what the president himself had done when faced with personal scandals seen as fatal to his presidential campaigns: stay in and fight.

Mr. Poindexter continued to work full time as an apprentice instructor throughout his primary campaign. He tried to make his own relatable life story part of his pitch to win over working-class Trump voters.

“I never got in this race to run because Max Miller is terrible in his personal life,” he said in an interview. “I got in it to run because of policies that hurt us.”

Despite the accusations, Mr. Miller was never fully deserted by House Republican leaders. Once it became clear there was no way to replace him on the ballot, they quietly spent more than $5 million to defend his seat, according to the ad-tracking service AdImpact.

item.title: With 2 Big Wins, Democrats May Have Put Ohio Back in Play
item.description:
Two years ago, Sherrod Brown lost the U.S. Senate seat he had held for three terms in Ohio when President Trump and the Republicans routed Democrats across the country. Now he is back, and deep-red Ohio may be back as a swing state.

“We made Ohio competitive after decades of Republican control,” Kathleen Clyde, the Ohio Democratic Committee Chair, shouted at a victory party in Columbus on Tuesday night. The Democrats had two big wins to celebrate: Mr. Brown beat the Republican incumbent, Senator Jon Husted, and Dr. Amy Acton defeated Vivek Ramaswamy, the billionaire former biotech executive, in the governor’s race.

Ohio was officially in play as a potential bellwether in the 2028 presidential campaign.

“If we’re still talking about the affordability of life, if we’re still talking about the affordability of housing, that does put Ohio back into the conversation,” David Niven, a professor of political science at the University of Cincinnati, said on Tuesday in anticipation of Democratic wins.

Ohio was once so representative of the national mood that it voted for the winning presidential candidate regardless of party in every election from 1964 to 2016. (And the state inspired the old political saw “As Ohio goes, so goes the nation.”)

John Kerry would have been elected president in 2004 had he won Ohio and its electoral votes, despite losing the popular vote to George W. Bush. Barack Obama won Ohio comfortably against John McCain in 2008. His margin was tighter against Mitt Romney in 2012, but Ohio carried Mr. Obama over the top in the Electoral College, sealing his re-election.

Mr. Trump’s victories in Ohio in 2016, 2020 and 2024 — particularly his 11-point win against Kamala Harris — made the state seem out of reach for Democrats. But there had been signs, even before the midterms, that things were changing, chiefly because of the economy.

“I’ve seen a shift in mind-set,” said Patrick Moran, the president of the American Federation of State, County and Municipal Employees, a union that represents 1.4 million workers nationwide, including 100,000 in Ohio, who hold jobs like school bus driver, sanitation worker and janitor. “People are angry, and they have a right to be angry. Because they can’t afford anything anymore.”

Mr. Moran was at a rally on Sunday for Dr. Acton and Mr. Brown outside Cleveland at a United Auto Workers’ union hall, Local 1250, which represents members who build engines for the Ford Expedition and the Ford Explorer. “We have Republican members who are stepping up and saying, ‘I can’t do this anymore, this is out of control.’” The president, he added, “made $1.4 billion while in office.”

Mr. Trump won Ohio three times by making inroads with unions and other blue collar workers, once the foundation of Mr. Brown’s — and Democrats’ — base. In Mr. Brown’s first campaign for Senate in 2006, he won Mahoning County, which includes the industrial city of Youngstown, by nearly 47 points over the Republican incumbent, Mike DeWine. In 2024, Mr. Brown lost the county by 0.2 percentage points to Bernie Moreno, showing how much defections of blue collar voters to Mr. Trump had hurt Democrats.

On Tuesday, Mr. Brown was winning Mahoning County by seven points, with 95 percent of the county’s results in. He also took his first victory in Delaware County, a longtime suburban Republican stronghold outside Columbus, winning by four points.

At a Skyline Chili restaurant in Delaware County, Amanda Volenick, a 39-year-old Democrat who had voted for Mr. Brown and Dr. Acton, said she thought the county was changing. She was having lunch with her brother, Jared Acker.

“Our parents are still huge Trump supporters,” Ms. Volenick, a nurse, said. “A lot of our family in that generation just voted a straight Republican ticket.” She was raised in an evangelical home, she said, and her parents thought Republicans were uniquely religious.

At another table, Matt Morris, a 50-year-old Republican, said he had voted for Mr. Trump in 2016 but not in 2020 or 2024. “I think he’s an idiot,” he said. In 2016, he said he “agreed with some of the stuff he was trying to do.”

He continued: “But he runs his mouth. Now he’s just serving his ego.’’

A friend Mr. Morris was having lunch with, a Republican who had voted for Mr. Trump three times, said he voted this year for Mr. Ramaswamy and Mr. Husted. He did not want to talk or give his name and got up quickly to pay his bill.

In another closely watched race in Ohio, Representative Max Miller, a Republican from the Cleveland area, lost his seat to Brian Poindexter, a Democrat. Mr. Miller had been accused of physically abusing his ex-wife, who is Senator Moreno’s daughter; he denied the accusation.

The one slightly positive sign, if it could be called that, for Ohio Republicans is that their losses were narrower compared with those in some other battleground states. Mr. Brown was winning overall by three points, with 91 percent of votes counted. Dr. Acton was winning by six points.

Robin Brilla, of Parma, a large Cleveland suburb, said she voted straight Republican on Tuesday, hoping to stave off any possible third impeachment of Mr. Trump. Ms. Brilla, 68, said she saw Mr. Trump as a defender of her values and way of life. She cited the Supreme Court’s overturning of Roe v. Wade as a key promise kept by the president.

“I’m a Christian, that’s my worldview,” she said. “And that’s something I agree with morally.”

In Brecksville, an affluent Cleveland suburb, Jane Molina, 53, said she was also a reliable Republican voter — once. But in the 2024 presidential election and in Tuesday’s midterms, she cast her ballot entirely for Democrats.

“Up until about 10 years ago I voted pretty much straight Republican,” Ms. Molina said after voting on Tuesday. “I hated politics. I didn’t pay attention. I didn’t understand it. I just knew that was what my mom was doing.”

From 2016 onward, Ms. Molina said, she started following the political news cycle and disliked what she saw from conservatives, particularly Mr. Trump.

“Now I vote straight Democrat,” she said.

For his part, Mr. Brown was not yet willing to declare Ohio a swing state. “I’m not a pundit,” he said soon after polls had opened on Tuesday. “But I do know that Amy Acton and I are going to win.”

He was at home in Columbus and had answered his wife’s cellphone while she was out of the room. While his campaign did not want him gabbing with the national media on Election Day — local media interviews would potentially bring in more last-minute votes — he seemed eager to talk.

His wife, Connie Schultz, a former Pulitzer Prize-winning columnist for The Cleveland Plain Dealer, soon arrived and took her phone back. “He just wants to talk to everybody right now,” she said. “He’s bouncing off the walls. We told him to go down and work out on his bike for a little bit.”

She, for one, thought that Mr. Trump’s unpopularity and the wins for her husband and Dr. Acton could make Ohio competitive again.

As Dr. Acton said at the victory party on Tuesday, “As Ohio goes, so goes the nation.”

Jessica Contrera contributed reporting from Columbus, Ohio, and Patrick Cooley from Brecksville and Parma, Ohio.

item.title: Historic Midterm Rout Serves as a Sweeping Rebuke of Trump Era
item.description:
President Trump implored voters over the course of the midterm campaign to “pretend I’m on the ballot.” He said it not once, not twice, but 47 times this fall.

And voters did — just not the way he hoped.

The Democratic wave in the congressional elections on Tuesday amounted to a stinging rebuke of a deeply unpopular president after more than a decade in which he has dominated the national stage. More than any of his predecessors, Mr. Trump deliberately made the midterm contest a referendum on himself, only to pay the price.

The electoral backlash extended even into deep red states and indicated that Mr. Trump has lost his hold over the coalition that lifted him to the White House twice. Frustrated by high gas prices, an intractable war with Iran and allegations of flagrant profiteering by Mr. Trump and members of his circle, voters who previously took a chance on an outsider promising change either rejected his party or stayed home.

As of early Wednesday morning, the Democratic margin of victory in the overall national vote for House seats was expected to be about 13 percentage points, the largest that either party has lodged in a congressional election since at least 1976, according to estimates by The New York Times. It will dwarf even the margins that the Republicans won in their two big landslide victories of modern times when they defeated congressional Democrats when Bill Clinton held the White House in 1994 and Barack Obama was president in 2010.

Thanks to redistricting, that margin may not translate into as many seats as the winners gained in those watershed years. Gerrymandered House districts leave far fewer seats available for poaching by the other party than in the past. But the overall margin of Democratic victory indicates that while the president has two more years left in office and can still wield power to great effect, Americans are signaling the beginning of the end of the Trump era.

“It’s basically a repudiation of Trump and the Republicans and what they’ve done for the last two years,” said Douglas B. Sosnik, who was White House political director for Mr. Clinton and closely tracked the races this fall. “I do think starting tomorrow, we’re in this new phase and it’s a transition phase and it will last two years. And it will be much more volatile than the last two years.”

Mr. Trump quickly tried to save face by insisting that the rout by Democrats was not really a rejection of him since he was not actually on the ballot — never mind that he told voters repeatedly to vote as if he were.

“I wasn’t on the ticket, and because I wasn’t on the ticket, we couldn’t get enough people out to vote,” he told The Times in an interview Tuesday night.

Even many Republicans would roll their eyes at that assertion, as this was a campaign that revolved so demonstrably around Mr. Trump.

It was Mr. Trump who decided to start a war with Iran that jolted energy markets and sent prices at the pump soaring. It was Mr. Trump who chose the candidates, the issues, the strategy and the message.

It was Mr. Trump who demanded complete loyalty from a party whose candidates were nervous about distancing themselves from him. And it was Mr. Trump who has shrugged off questions about the ethics of his moneymaking in office, helping propel voter concerns about corruption.

The defeat of two Senate Republican candidates that he personally selected over potentially more electable contenders in deep red states — Ken Paxton in Texas and Darline Graham in South Carolina — demonstrated the consequences of his interventions. His push to throw out the normal process and redraw House districts in the middle of the decade to try to stack the deck for Republicans backfired.

Many voters told pollsters and interviewers that they felt hoodwinked by Mr. Trump, believing that he was going to bring down prices and not start new wars. They expected him to close the border, but bristled at what they saw as heavy-handed arrests of people living in the country for years. They rebelled against the tariffs that increased costs for consumers.

The way Mr. Trump spent his last day before the election proved to be a metaphor for how out of sync his political instincts were with the season. Instead of emphasizing plans to address the cost of living worries weighing on many voters, he delivered his final pre-election address at the Reflecting Pool, talking about algae and pipes. It was a vivid reminder of his obsession with pet construction projects in Washington, despite the warning signs of how it rankled voters — as if Richard M. Nixon had made his final pre-election speech in front of the Watergate complex.

Even if Trumpism may be receding, Mr. Trump has the power of the presidency for two more years and will do everything he can to remain a dominant voice for as long as he can. His allies warned against assuming that he is a spent force.

“Trump’s critics have written his political obituary before and been wrong every time,” said David McIntosh, president of the Club for Growth, a group that promotes conservative economic policies.

“The fix is Republicans getting back to our principles,” he added. “That’s how we win in 2028.”

There is, of course, a natural tendency to draw great lessons from a big midterm wave, to assume that it represents a fundamental shift in the American electorate. It certainly may. But history has seen plenty of examples when it did not last long. And it remains to be seen whether Tuesday’s results signal a broader ideological shift among voters.

The post-Watergate wave of 1974 was thought to presage a long winter in the political wilderness for Republicans, but Ronald Reagan brought the party back to the White House just six years later. The 1994 and 2010 Republican sweeps were expected to presage the end of the Clinton and Obama presidencies, but both came back to win re-election handily two years later.

Lynn Vavrek, a professor of American politics and public policy at the University of California, Los Angeles, said the most important factor in the election was sky-high gas prices so it may not follow that the country’s political character has profoundly changed.

“It doesn’t mean the MAGA coalition is crumbling,” she said. “Does it mean the shine has come off Donald Trump a little bit? Yes. Are people less enamored of him? I think the answer to that is yes.” But she said it does not necessarily mean that Republicans are going to abandon the “identity-inflected policies” on issues like immigration and diversity that have animated the party under Mr. Trump.

This is, after all, a fundamentally altered party, one that Mr. Trump forged in his own image, empowering those who defer to him and purging those who exhibit independence. “We don’t know how the president’s going to react, but thus far we’ve only seen members of his party acquiesce to him,” said Christina M. Greer, a political science professor at Fordham University.

Joe Grogan, who served as Mr. Trump’s domestic policy adviser in his first term, said that regardless of the election results, the president has changed the political landscape by advancing issues that were not adequately addressed enough before, like pushing for better trade deals and securing greater military spending by NATO allies. The party, he said, is not moving back to what it once was.

“We’re still in Trump’s party, regardless of what happens tonight,” Mr. Grogan, now at Covington & Burling, said before the polls closed. “People who expect Trumpism to get repudiated I think are mistaken. There will be some debates that I think will be healthy for the party. But I just don’t see there being a huge wellspring for the party to go back to the one that George W. Bush led for two successful elections.”

At the same time, Democrats will debate how to interpret their victory. Their main identity this year was simply being against Mr. Trump, which was more than enough. But progressives will say that it was energy on the left that powered the success, while moderates will say it was the appeal to disaffected Republicans in states like Texas and Kansas that was crucial.

“The biggest story is non-MAGA Republicans have broken with the Republican Party,” said Rahm Emanuel, a former Democratic Chicago mayor and ambassador exploring a run for president. “The question is do we want to make this election transactional or transformational? What we do in 2027 will determine that.”

James Blanchard, who was first elected to Congress in the post-Watergate Democratic sweep of 1974 and later served as governor of Michigan, said this year’s election felt similar to that historic year. But he said that does not mean that American politics will return to the way they were before Mr. Trump. “We can never go back, unfortunately,” he said. “We’re going to have to go forward.”

“It’s the end of Trump,” he added, “even though he’s still going to be there."

item.title: Five Things to Know About Hakeem Jeffries
item.description:
On the frigid evening of President Trump’s inauguration last year, after the vindicated president swept back into power and immediately pardoned nearly all of the Jan. 6 rioters, Representative Hakeem Jeffries, Democrat of New York, gathered his top lieutenants for a quiet dinner in Washington.

In a private back room at Osteria Morini, an Italian restaurant on the Anacostia River, Mr. Jeffries, the relatively untested Democratic leader, and his team strategized for hours about how to use their limited power in the minority to check a newly empowered president who now had control of both houses of Congress.

Mr. Jeffries, according to a person who attended the dinner, was preoccupied with a single imperative.

“We just have to win,” he said firmly. “If we don’t win in 2026, it’s over.”

On Tuesday, Democrats did just that, claiming the House majority and putting Mr. Jeffries, 56, on the precipice of making history as the first Black speaker of the House. His actions will determine how effective Democrats can be in checking Mr. Trump’s power, and help set the agenda for the 2028 presidential campaign.

Here are five things to know about Mr. Jeffries.

Mr. Jeffries grew up in a working-class home in the Crown Heights section of Brooklyn in the 1980s, when the now-gentrified neighborhood was a hotbed of Black activism, but also overrun with crime and unrest associated with the crack cocaine epidemic.

The son of a social worker and a substance abuse counselor, who became a high-powered litigator, Mr. Jeffries grew up in a house that was described by longtime associates as teeming with Black nationalist ideas. His uncle, Leonard Jeffries, a professor at the City College of New York, was associated with the Afrocentrism movement and often expressed extreme views on the subject.

Mr. Jeffries and his brother, Hasan Kwame Jeffries, a history professor at the Ohio State University, were pushed by their churchgoing parents to excel above all else.

“When Hakeem was growing up, Myrtle Avenue was known as Murder Avenue,” recalled Lupe Todd-Medina, one of his longtime political advisers. “It was not a place white people wanted to go. He grew up in this bubble of love, with lots of aunties around him. That also helped shape who he is.”

His mother and his aunt joined the Cornerstone Baptist Church, a Black house of worship, in the 1960s, and the congregation and its pastors became an important force in shaping Mr. Jeffries’s early life. Growing up, he served as an usher there. His grandmother predicted that he would one day become a pastor.

Mr. Jeffries has said that he has been motivated since entering law school by fights over racial justice. If all goes as expected and he is elected in January as the first Black speaker, he would be second in line to the presidency.

“That might be the thing that matters the most to him — breaking the glass,” Ms. Todd-Medina said.

At a victory party on Tuesday night, he ended his remarks with a note of hometown pride. “We made it, Brooklyn,” he said, “we made it.”

Former Speaker Nancy Pelosi never exactly groomed her mentees, but she had a small circle of loyal House Democrats around her whom she viewed as potential successors. For a time, the top spot in that group was occupied by Chris Van Hollen, then a representative from Maryland. When Mr. Van Hollen won a Senate seat and left the House, Ms. Pelosi looked to Representative Joe Crowley of New York as someone who operated in her mold and could lead the caucus in the future.

But Mr. Crowley was defeated in a 2018 upset by Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez. After that, some of Ms. Pelosi’s closest allies included Representatives Ben Ray Luján of New Mexico and Adam B. Schiff of California, both of whom went on to serve in the Senate.

Mr. Jeffries was never one of her people. But when he was elected by Democrats in 2018 to be the chairman of their caucus, essentially their chief messaging official and No. 5 leader, he was widely seen as having the potential to be the first Black speaker.

And four years later, when Ms. Pelosi acceded to calls to relinquish her role as the top Democrat, Mr. Jeffries quickly emerged as his colleagues’ top choice to take her place. He was elected House Democratic leader by acclamation after the 2022 midterm elections.

Mr. Jeffries’s Democratic colleagues have always elected him to leadership posts by unanimous votes, and he is not expected to face a challenge for the job of speaker. But that does not mean that they are uniformly thrilled about his elevation to become the most powerful man in the House.

Though he is seen as a fresh face compared with the octogenarians who led Democrats in the House until recently, Mr. Jeffries is substantially more moderate than Ms. Pelosi and the progressives who are the largest bloc in the caucus. He is viewed as an establishment figure at a time when many Democratic voters are rejecting their party’s entrenched power structure.

And some Democrats regard Mr. Jeffries as overly cautious, according to interviews with a half-dozen officials who spoke on the condition of anonymity to offer an unvarnished view of his standing.

They questioned whether he had the instincts to sustain the kind of fights that Democrats will need to show voters they can wage and win, now that they have regained some power in Washington.

Some House Democrats also said they had been surprised over the years when they did not hear much directly from Mr. Jeffries, even after successes or struggles. They had grown accustomed to Ms. Pelosi, who would constantly work the phones to keep her finger on the pulse of the caucus, often congratulating or commiserating with lawmakers as she quizzed them about what they were hearing. But Ms. Pelosi effectively operated as both the speaker and the whip.

These days, the duties are more divided and it is Representative Katherine M. Clark of Massachusetts, the No. 2 who is in line to become the first female majority leader, who generally serves as whip and takes on a lot of member management.

Some of Mr. Jeffries’s allies said that they expected him to act more aggressively and decisively in his new job.

“When you’re the speaker, you become the engine of the vote,” said Representative Gregory W. Meeks, Democrat of New York and one of Mr. Jeffries’s most trusted lieutenants. “Hakeem is ready to do just that. In the minority, your role is not as commanding.”

Many democratic socialist candidates elected this year view Mr. Jeffries with particular aversion, regarding him as an establishment politician who has held back some of their progressive goals.

They also see him as too closely aligned with AIPAC, the pro-Israel lobbying group that has come to be seen by many Democrats as politically radioactive. The radio host Charlamagne Tha God has mocked him as “AIPAC Shakur.”

Mr. Jeffries bristles at the notion that he is beholden to any outside special interest group.

“Nobody can point to a single instance of me taking a vote that had anything to do with being influenced by any outside group,” he said in an interview earlier this year.

Still, Mr. Jeffries will face a major test next year from a progressive bloc of lawmakers who want Democrats to unite around ending military aid to Israel, which has bitterly divided the party. He will face competing pressure from more centrist Democrats, who have privately warned him that the party will get flattened if he goes too far in appeasing the left.

Mr. Jeffries is already cognizant of a need for Democrats to recalibrate their position on Israel. The question is how far he will be willing to go.

Earlier this year, he opposed a measure that nearly half of House Democrats backed that would have terminated U.S. aid to Israel. But in a letter announcing his position, he conceded that there were good reasons to back the measure and asserted that “a meaningful change in direction is needed” in the relationship between the United States and Israel.

Mr. Jeffries, a Generation X leader in a Congress still filled with baby boomers, has made hip-hop culture a central part of his public persona, often peppering his speeches with rap lyrics.

During Mr. Trump’s 2020 impeachment trial, Mr. Jeffries ended his somber presentation with a lyric by the rapper and fellow Brooklynite Biggie Smalls: “And if you don’t know, now you know.”

At a news conference in February, he quoted the rapper Jay-Z, while railing against redistricting in Texas.

“At what point will Republican extremists come to the conclusion that your reach ain’t long enough and your peeps ain’t strong enough?” he said.

He turned again to inspiration from Jay-Z in March, at a news conference related to the government shutdown.

“But for us, difficult takes a day, impossible takes a week,” Mr. Jeffries said, quoting a Jay-Z guest verse on Kanye West’s “Diamonds from Sierra Leone.”

item.title: Democrat Defeats Nunn in Iowa, Scoring a Key House Pickup
item.description:
Sarah Trone Garriott, a Democratic state senator and Lutheran minister, defeated Representative Zach Nunn, Republican of Iowa, according to The Associated Press, flipping a key seat to help her party win control of the House.

Ms. Trone Garriott’s victory over Mr. Nunn, a two-term incumbent who had closely aligned himself with President Trump, was a major breakthrough for Democrats in a district that Mr. Nunn had won twice. Republicans had invested millions of dollars there to defend one of their most vulnerable incumbents.

It was also a rebuke of the Trump administration’s economic agenda in a politically divided stretch of central and southern Iowa, where Ms. Trone Garriott had made rising costs, health care cuts and the economic consequences of the war in Iran central to her campaign.

Throughout the race, Ms. Trone Garriott sought to cast Mr. Nunn as a politician more concerned with protecting the president and his wealthy supporters than with the financial struggles of ordinary Iowans.

“Families are paying too much for groceries, health care and child care, and people are tired of politicians in Washington who look out for themselves,” she said last month, summarizing her central argument.

Her victory demonstrated the potency of that message in Iowa’s Third Congressional District, which encompasses Des Moines, its fast-growing suburbs and a broad swath of rural Iowa where Republicans have maintained considerable political strength.

A former Air Force intelligence officer, Mr. Nunn, 47, had spent much of his time in Congress as a steadfast supporter of Mr. Trump’s agenda. He repeatedly backed legislation that cut federal Medicaid spending, declined to break with the president over his sweeping tariffs and for months supported the war in Iran.

But as polling showed growing dissatisfaction with the war and its economic consequences, Mr. Nunn sought to distance himself from the administration. In September, after repeatedly rejecting efforts to restrict the president’s military authority, he joined a small group of Republicans who voted to curtail Mr. Trump’s ability to continue waging the war.

The shift was not enough to save him.

Ms. Trone Garriott, who had opposed the war, repeatedly tied the military operation to rising gasoline and fertilizer prices, arguing that Iowa families and farmers were paying the price for a conflict Congress had never authorized.

She also attacked Mr. Nunn’s support for the Republican domestic policy law that reduced Medicaid spending, accusing him of endangering access to health care in rural communities already struggling to keep hospitals and clinics open.

Ms. Trone Garriott, who defeated a powerful Republican incumbent to win her State Senate seat, held public town halls in all 21 counties of the congressional district, making her accessibility to constituents a central contrast with Mr. Nunn.

She also proved to be a formidable fund-raiser, bringing in more than $8 million by late October, substantially more than Mr. Nunn’s approximately $6 million. Outside Republican groups poured millions into defending his seat even as some of the party’s most powerful super PACs withdrew support from another vulnerable Iowa incumbent, Representative Mariannette Miller-Meeks.

Mr. Nunn had demonstrated considerable political staying power, rooted in his popularity beyond the Democratic stronghold of Des Moines. But Ms. Trone Garriott appealed to suburban voters and sought to cut into the large margins Republicans traditionally enjoyed in rural communities.
